events.event_narrative: High wind was reported along the south side of Casper. Wind gusts of 70 and 68 mph were reported along Wyoming Boulevard and Hat Six Road, respectively.
A maximum wind gust of 63 mph was reported by the ASOS at Southwest Wyoming Regional Airport. A separate 63 mph wind gust was reported at the Snow Springs RAWS site southeast of Rock Springs.
High wind occurred across much of northern Johnson County. The peak reported wind gust was 69 mph at the Johnson County Airport.
The wind sensor at Red Canyon along Wyoming Highway 28 reported maximum wind gusts of 80 mph.
The ASOS at Hunt Field in Lander recorded a wind gust of 58 mph.
Very heavy snow fell in the Teton Range. Some of the highest totals included 37 inches at the Surprise Meadow SNOTEL site and 36 inches at the Jackson Hole Mountain Resort.
Two of the highest snow totals were 24 inches at Commissary Ridge and 22 inches at the Cottonwood Creek SNOTEL site.
Snowfall amounts through the Jackson Valley ranged from 24 inches at Moose to 11 inches at Teton Village to 6 inches in the town of Jackson.
Snowfall amounts in the Star Valley ranged from 12 inches at Afton to 18 inches near Alpine.
Snowfall amounts in the Upper Green River Foothills ranged from around 12 inches at Pinedale to 23 inches at Bondurant.
Heavy snow fell in the western Wind River Mountains. The highest estimated total was 21 inches at the Kendall Ranger Station SNOTEL site.
Heavy snow fell in southern Lincoln County. Some notable amounts included 14 inches at Cokeville and 12 inches in Kemmerer.
Heavy snow fell in Dubois, where 10 inches of new snow was measured. Amounts dropped sharply farther to the south and east along US Highway 26.
Winds gusted as high as 63 mph at the Snow Springs RAWS site. The ASOS at Southwest Wyoming Regional Airport near Rock Springs recorded a wind gust of 60 mph.
A maximum wind gust of 83 mph was reported at Red Canyon along Wyoming Highway 28. The Wind River RAWS site had a maximum wind gust of 78 mph.

High wind occurred in portions of Natrona County. The peak wind gust reported was 77 mph along Wyoming Boulevard to the south of Casper. The ASOS at Casper/Natrona County International Airport reported a wind gust of 60 mph.
A maximum wind gust of 83 mph was reported at the Fales Rock RAWS site.

Very strong wind occurred in portions of the Cody Foothills. To the west of Clark, there were many wind gusts exceeding hurricane force with a maximum gust of 107 mph. A 65 mph wind gust was reported along Wyoming Highway 120 to the north of Meeteetse.
New snowfall amounts around Casper generally ranged from 5 to 9 inches.
A 58 mph wind gust occurred at the Dubois Airport.
A 58 mph wind gust occurred at Hunt Field in Lander.
High winds, with a peak gust of 65 mph, occurred at Thermopolis.
A maximum wind gust of 65 mph was reported near Tisdale Divide along Interstate 25 in southern Johnson County.
High wind gusts occurred in typically wind-prone areas on the south side of Casper. The maximum wind gust was 67 mph along Wyoming Boulevard.
Wind speeds were sustained at over 50 mph for more than an hour along the Chief Joseph Highway. The maximum wind gust registered was 88 mph.
Winds gusted as high as 85 mph to the west of Clark.
A peak gust of 75 mph was clocked at a mesonet station west of Clark near the foothills of the Absaroka Range.
The ASOS at Central Wyoming Regional Airport in Riverton measured a maximum wind gust of 64 mph.
A 60 mph wind gust was measured at the Johnson County Airport near Buffalo.
Winds were sustained over 50 mph along the Chief Joseph Highway. A mesonet anemometer recorded a maximum wind gust of 89 mph.
High winds occurred in portions of the Cody Foothills. The maximum wind gust reported was 64 mph at Wapiti.

Cooperative weather observers measured anywhere 8 to 10 inches of snow from around Ten Sleep south toward Big Trails. Additional reports indicated most areas in eastern Washakie County received 7 to 13 inches of snow. Amounts dropped sharply farther west with only an inch of new snow around Worland.
Trained spotters measured anywhere from 6 to 11 inches of snow around the Lander Foothills. At the Lander airport, Hunt Field, 5 inches of snow was measured.
High wind blew for several hours along Chief Joseph Highway with a maximum wind gust of 95 mph.
Wind gusts over 60 mph were reported in the Cody Foothills, with a maximum gust of 64 mph along Wyoming Highway 120 over Meeteetse Rim north of Meeteetse.
Please see Episode for a description.
Some notable temperatures less than 20 below zero in western Natrona County included 23 below zero at Powder River and 22 below zero at Natrona.
The weather station near the Johnson / Sheridan County border recorded a low temperature of 20 below zero.
Some of the notable temperatures in Washakie County included 29 below zero near Big Trails south of Ten Sleep, and 21 below zero at Worland Municipal Airport.
Some of the more notable low temperatures included 26 below zero near Buffalo Bill Reservoir and 24 below zero at Wapiti.
A cooperative weather observer northeast of Thermopolis reported a low temperature of 20 below zero.

Typically known as the Valley of the Warm Winds, the area around Dubois was anything but that. The low temperature bottomed out at 22 below zero at Dubois and 20 below zero at Crowheart, while the nearby mountain locale of Union Pass dropped to 28 below zero.

Heavy rainfall and melting snow caused rapid rises on the North Fork and Middle Fork of the Powder River near Kaycee, Barnum, and Mayoworth.  Both branches of the river flooded. Rainfall totals ranged from around 3.25 inches to near 5.00 inches. A report from near Mayoworth indicated 6.36 inches fell over three days.||In Kaycee, the arena at Harold Jarrard Park was flooded, but no damage was reported in town. Sandbagging efforts began two days in advance of the flood and protected area homes which were at no time evacuated. The flooded areas were mainly comprised of agricultural lowlands or areas within the historic flood plain.
Both forks of Medicine Lodge Creek were out of their banks following heavy rainfall of around one-half inch which occurred in combination with snowmelt from the Bighorn Mountains.
Locally heavy snow fell in around Rock Springs, with 6 to 9 inches commonplace. Amounts dropped sharply farther west with only 2 to 3 inches around Green River.
A combination of snow and blowing snow led to closure of US Highway 189 south of Kemmerer for several hours.

Ten Sleep Creek was out of its banks near the town of Ten Sleep as a result of snowmelt runoff and heavy rain. A nearby section of the Nowood River was also running high. Rainfall totals ranged from around 1.25 to near 2.00 inches.

The combination of heavy rainfall of three to five inches and snowmelt from the nearby Bighorn Mountains caused Rock and Clear creeks to flood near Buffalo. The high water levels flooded some homes along Rock Creek where it flows beneath Interstate 90.

Flood waters from Elkhorn Creek damaged Strube Loop Road and inundated neighboring areas to a depth of two feet across a 30-foot wide swath. Some buildings at the Lion's Camp on Casper Mountain sustained damage. During the afternoon, Elkhorn Creek was reported to be 50 yards wide and two feet deep in spots. The creek eventually flooded portions of two fairways at Casper Country Club as the waterway emptied down the north-face of Casper Mountain.

The North Fork of the Shoshone River crested around 8.5 feet about one-half foot above flood stage. This caused state park officials to sandbag a campground at Buffalo Bill State Park west of Cody. The flooding occurred during the early morning hours as snowmelt water from the previous day progressed downstream.
A trained spotter reported quarter sized hail.
Nickel sized hail was reported by a spotter along U.S. Highway 16 northeast of Buffalo.
Hail of nickel to quarter size in diameter was reported by a motorist at exit 210 on Interstate 25. Visibility due to the hail and rain was near zero.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Tetons. The highest amount was 15 inches at the Grand Targhee SNOTEL site.
Snowfall amounts in the Jackson Valley ranged from 5 inches in the town of Jackson to 9 inches near Wilson.
Snowfall amounts around the Star Valley ranged from 6 inches in Alpine to nearly 10 inches at the Star Valley Ranch.
Heavy snow fell in the Salt River and Wyoming ranges. The highest amount recorded was 18 inches the the Spring Creek SNOTEL site.
Snowfall amounts around Lander generally ranged from 5 to 9 inches, including 7 inches the at the Lander Airport.
A trained spotter measured 7 inches of snow in Dubois.
Trained spotters measured 7 to 9 inches of new snow around the city of Riverton. Amounts dropped sharply to the west and east of town.
Please see episode for a description.
Widespread low temperatures of at least 20 below zero were reported in Yellowstone National Park. The lowest temperatures reported was 43 below zero at Grant Village.
Temperatures fell as low as 17 below zero in Hot Springs County.
The low temperature of 19 below zero was the coldest temperature reported so late in the year. A weather station in the town of Worland reported a low temperature of 21 below zero.
Several locations in the Jackson Valley reported low temperatures less than 20 below zero. This included 23 below zero at the Jackson Hole airport.

A combination of fresh snow and a clear sky brought very cold temperatures to the Wind River Basin. The low of 13 below zero at the Riverton ASOS was the all-time coldest temperature so late in the season. Temperatures in the town of Riverton were even colder, falling as low as 23 below zero.
The low temperature of 15 below zero at the Lander Airport broke the old record low of 11 below zero set in 1948.
Some of lowest temperatures recorded included 32 below zero near Sweetwater Station and 23 below zero at Jeffrey City.

Numerous locations around Natrona County saw low temperatures fall under 20 below zero. The low temperature of 25 below zero at the Casper-Natrona County International Airport was the all-time record low for the month of March.
Very cold low temperatures were recorded in the Star Valley. The lowest temperatures was 31 below zero at the Afton airport.
Very cold temperatures occurred throughout the area. This included a low temperature of 20 below zero at the Pinedale airport.
Very cold temperatures occurred in the Green River Basin. Notable temperatures included 24 below zero at Daniel and 22 below zero at the Big Piney Airport.
Very cold temperatures occurred in southern Lincoln County. Notable temperatures included 20 below zero at Cokeville.
Locations in East Sweetwater County saw temperatures fall below 20 below zero, including 24 below zero at Bitter Creek along Interstate 80.
A maximum wind gust of 69 mph was reported along Highway 120 near Meeteetse. Other notable wind gusts included 66 mph in Dry Creek and 60 mph at Clark.
A maximum wind gust of 65 mph was reported along Interstate 80 in Green River.
A maximum wind gust of 63 mph was reported at the Southwest Wyoming Regional airport near Rock Springs. A 61 mph gust was reported along Interstate 80 near the Sweetwater-Carbon county border.
A 61 mph wind gust was reported at the Jackson Hole airport.
A maximum wind gust of 88 mph was reported at the summit of the Jackson Hole Ski resort.

A maximum wind gust of 72 mph was reported at the Johnson County airport near Buffalo. Numerous locations along Interstates 25 and 90 had wind gusts past 60 mph, resulting in very difficult travel conditions, especially for high profile vehicles.
The RAWS site at Fales Rock had a maximum wind gust of 88 mph.

A maximum wind gust of 69 mph was reported at the Natrona County Airport west of Casper. Numerous wind gusts over 60 mph were reported along numerous wind sensors along Interstate 25 as well as US 20 26.
A maximum wind gust of 67 mph was reported at Crowheart.
A maximum wind gust of 68 mph was reported at the Riverton airport.
A maximum wind gust of 79 mph was reported at a weather station in Sinks Canyon. The high wind blew down a fence at a ranch. The Lander airport had a wind gust of 58 mph.
Trained spotters reported 5 to 7 inches around northern Johnson County. The snow combined with wind gusts up over 50 mph to bring very difficult travel conditions and some road closures.
A CoCoRaHs spotter reported 6 inches of snow north of Kaycee. The snow combined with wind gusts up over 50 mph to bring very difficult travel conditions and some road closures.
Trained spotters reported anywhere from 10 inches of new snow at Star Valley Ranch to 13 inches of snow near Thayne.
A CoCoRahs spotter reported 8 inches of snow in Lovell. The snow was blown around by winds over 50 mph at times and brought very difficult travel conditions.
A trained spotter measured 8.5 inches of snow in Thermopolis.

Heavy snow combined with winds gusting as high as 76 mph produced blizzard conditions across northern Johnson County that lead to numerous road closures. Notable wind gusts included 76 mph at the Johnson County airport and 77 mph along Interstate 90.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Big Horn Range. The highest amount was 16 inches at the Middle Powder SNOTEL site.
At the Cloud Peak SNOTEL site, 12 inches of new snow fell.
A COOP observer reported 10.7 inches of snow at Sweetwater Station at the Intersections of Highways 287 and 135. The snow combined with strong winds to bring some road closures.
Heavy snow fell in portions of Natrona County. The highest amount was on the south side of Casper where 9.5 inches of snow fell.
The Casper Mountain SNOTEL site had 16 inches of new snow.

A trained spotter reported 11.5 inches of snow near Meeteetse. Amounts dropped sharply further north with only 2 inches around Cody. The snow combined with wind gusts over 60 mph to bring very difficult travel conditions at times.
Snowfall amounts ranged from 12 to 18 inches of new snow above 8000 feet of elevation.
Time of event is based on observations sites in the region, and the time of discovery of trees down.
An 82 mph wind gust was reported at the East Entrance of Yellowstone Park. Many trees were downed and power was knocked out. The road was closed until 7 pm due to an avalanche.
A 66 mph wind gust was reported at the Rock Springs Airport.
A 59 mph wind gust was reported at the Big Piney airport.
A trained spotter reported quarter size hail to the north of Basin along Highway 789.
A trained spotter reported nickel size hail to the west of Casper.
Wind gusts as high as 92 mph were recorded along Highway 28 near South Pass. A 77 mph gust was recorded at the Wind River RAWS site.
Wind gusted as high as 61 mph in Crowheart, WY.
Wind gusts as high as 60 mph were reported at the Sweetwater County Airport.
Heavy snow fell in northern portions of the Bighorn Mountains. The highest amount recorded was 25 inches the Bone Springs SNOTEL site. Amounts dropped further southward and in the lower elevations.
Favorable upslope easterly flow brought heavy snow to the southeastern Bighorn Range, especially above 8000 feet. The highest amounts reported was 33 inches at the Cloud Peak Reservoir SNOTEL site.
Favorable easterly upslope flow brought very heavy snow to the Absarokas. There were numerous reports of over 18 inches of snow with a maximum of 37 inches at the Marquette SNOTEL site.

Heavy snow fell in portions of the Wind River Range, mainly above 8000 feet. The highest amount was at the Hobbs Park SNOTEL site where 24 inches of new snow fell. Measured amounts elsewhere were 14 inches or less.
Heavy snow fell at the Parker Peak SNOTEL site where 24 inches of new snow was measured.
A trained spotter reported quarter-sized hail in Midwest, WY.
A reporter for a local newspaper sent a picture of a funnel cloud over the Owl Creek Mountains to the southwest of Thermopolis, WY.
In Park County, a trained spotter reported nickel-sized hail with a thunderstorm near Powell, WY.
Near Ucross, WY, ping pong ball sized hail was reported.
A 58 mph wind gust was reported at the South Bighorn County Airport.
Trees were damaged and a power line was downed in Midwest, WY.

A maximum wind gust of 61 mph was reported at the Johnson County Airport near Buffalo, WY. In the city of Buffalo, the public reported small limbs snapped off trees and a few shingles blown off roofs.
A 58 mph wind gust was reported near Wamsutter along Interstate 80.

Rain showers associated with a passing cold front mixed down strong low level winds to the surface in Natrona County. The strongest wind gust reported was 72 mph along Wyoming Boulevard south of Casper, WY. The Natrona County airport also had a wind gust of 64 mph.
A trained spotter reported quarter size hail near Barnum, WY.
A wind gust of 58 mph was reported at the Johnson County Airport near Buffalo, WY.
A wind gust of 59 mph was reported at the Sweetwater County Airport near Rock Springs, WY.

A combination of heavy rain and rapid snowmelt led to severe flooding in Yellowstone Park. Along the road to the northern entrance to Yellowstone Park, the road was completely washed out in several locations. Yellowstone National Park created an online video and picture album to highlight the extensive damage.

Part of the northeastern entrance road to Yellowstone National Park was washed out near the Soda Butte Picnic Area. There were also mudslides and downed trees in the area. Yellowstone National Park press releases estimated preliminary repair costs to be 25 million for the northeast entrance road.
The road between Tower Junction and Canyon Junction was closed by a mudslide on the road.
A section of road to the south of Canyon Village collapsed to heavy rain and flooding.
The river gage at Crowheart, WY along the Wind River peaked near 11  feet. The flooding remained in low-lying areas and caused no known damage.
The Wind River near Kinnear, WY peaked around 9 feet. The flooding was confined to low lying areas around the river and caused no known damage.
The Wind River at Riverton, WY peaked around 10 feet. The flood remained over low-lying areas near the river and caused no known damage.
Penny sized hail fell near exit 88 on Interstate 90.

A supercell thunderstorm moved over the Bridger Teton National Forest to the east of Jackson, WY. Strong outflow winds from the supercell downed hundreds of trees over an approximately 6 mile path. There was extensive damage to the Crystal Creek Campground, where people were trapped until the road could be cleared 24 hours later. The Grizzly Lake Trail and Gros Ventre River Road were affected by tree damage. Maximum wind gusts were estimated to be in the 80 to 120 mph range based on tree damage. This damage is in addition to the tornado that occurred at higher elevations to the southwest of this lower-elevation campground damage and road damage.
The public reported quarter size hail on Teton Pass.
The Teton County Emergency Manager reported a tree down in the town of Jackson, WY.
The USGS river gauge on the Lamar River near Tower Falls surged well above the previous record of 12.15', cresting near 16.79' around 6:30 AM MST, which is over 4' higher than the previous record.
A maximum wind gust of 64 mph was recorded at the Cowley Airport.
The Willow Creek RAWS weather sensor recorded a maximum wind gust of 64 mph.
A maximum wind gust of 63 mph was reported at the South Big Horn County Airport near Greybull.
A maximum wind gust of 61 mph was reported at the Johnson County Airport near Buffalo.
Several trees were blown over, knocking out power to around 350 customers in Daniel and Pinedale. Shingles were blown off of the Museum Of The Mountain Man.
A 74 mph wind gust was reported at the Lander airport.
A maximum wind gust of 59 mph was reported at the Lander airport.
Strong thunderstorm winds blew down trees onto power lines that caused power outages to 400 customers. A maximum wind gust of 68 mph was reported at the Powell airport.
The Sublette County Emergency Manager reported 4 powerline poles and 2 trees were downed by the strong wind gusts. Minor flooding also occurred in the area.

A tributary of Kitty Creek rose out of its banks and pushed mud and debris from the higher elevations onto local roads and a cabin area south of US Hwy 14 (North Fork Highway). A WYDOT official reported mud and debris were 3 feet deep in some locations just upstream along US Hwy 14. Many people were stranded in the area as local roads and the highway were impassable. A car was totaled when the driver attempted to drive through the flooded road. A private cabin was also damaged by the flooding. Hwy 14 was closed over the next 12 hours, opening back up the following morning.

On Tuesday evening, August 2, 2022 lightning struck a group of backpackers camped at Enos Lake in the Teton Wilderness. One person, a 22-year-old male, died in the incident, while another, an adult male, sustained major injuries. The lightning bolt reportedly hit the backpackers at camp. The men were part of a group of 14 adults on an organized wilderness trip. This information is directly from a Teton County Search and Rescue press release describing the event.

A thunderstorm produced a microburst that brought tree damage in the vicinity of Doyle Creek Campground to the south of Hazelton in the Bighorn Range. Several trees were uprooted or snapped off above the ground.

The ASOS weather station at the Riverton Airport (Central Wyoming Airport) observed record high temperatures on 6 consecutive days. Highs were 90 or greater on the first 8 days of the month. The high temperature of 100 F on September 4th is the all time high for September, as well as the latest date to reach 100 F on record.

The ASOS at the Lander Airport (Hunt Field Airport) recorded 6 consecutive days of record high temperatures over 90 degrees F. The high temperature of 99 F on September 4th is the all time record high for the month of September. Records at Lander date back to 1891.

The Rock Springs Airport (Southwest Wyoming Regional Airport) had 6 consecutive days of record high temperatures in the 90s. The high temperatures of 93 F on the 4th and 7th are now tied for the all time high temperature for the month of September.

The Casper Airport (Casper���Natrona County International Airport) had 7 consecutive days of high temperatures 90 F or greater. In addition, the high temperature of 100 F on September 4th is the all time high temperature for the month of September, and the first ever recorded 100 degree temperature in the month. Records at the site date back to 1947.

Record and near record temperatures were observed at the Johnson County Airport (near Buffalo, WY)  for the first 7 days of the month. The heat peaked on September 4th with a high temperature of 100 F. This is the all time high temperature for September, and the first ever recorded 100 degree F temperature for the month of September.

The month started with 7 consecutive days of high temperatures over 90 degrees at the Worland Municipal Airport. Most notable was the high of 102 F on September 4th, which broke the all time September high temperature.

At the Greybull Airport (South Big Horn County Airport) there were 7 consecutive days of high temperatures over 90 degrees to start the month. On the 4th and 7th, the all time September high temperature of 103 degrees F was set then tied. The 103 F on September 7th is now the latest 100 F or greater temperature for the site.

Record heat occurred at the Lake Yellowstone ASOS. Five consecutive days had high temperatures of 80 F or greater. On September 7th, a record high temperature of 83 degrees F broke the all time record high for September.

Record and near record temperatures occurred at the Big Piney-Marbleton Airport. On September 4th, 6th, and 7th, record high temperatures of 91 F set and then tied (twice) the all time high temperature for the month of September. September 7th is also the latest 90 degree F or greater temperature for this site.
No lightning was detected in the area, so this was technically not a thunderstorm at the time of the severe wind observation.
Nickel to quarter sized hail accumulated to a depth of three to four inches at Jenny Lake in Grand Teton National Park. One person received lacerations and several other people had welts.
A cooperative observer near Alta observed nickel sized hail.
Two trees were downed when a thunderstorm wind gust estimated at 70 mph struck a ranch near Boysen Reservoir.
Heavy snow fell in the higher elevations of Yellowstone National Park. The maximum amount of snow reported was 16 inches at the Thumb Divide SNOTEL site.
At the Grand Targhee SNOTEL site 13 inches of snow was reported.
A maximum wind gust of 89 mph was reported at the Wyoming Department of Transportation weather sensor at Red Canyon. The nearby Wind River RAWS site had a maximum wind gust of 80 mph.
The Lander airport had a maximum wind gust of 70 mph. In Lander, a tree was downed on Shoshone Street.
Along Wyoming Boulevard to the south of Casper, maximum wind gusts of 60 mph were reported.

Several months after this event, Bridger Teton National Forest staff reached out to the NWS Riverton office and shared images and helicopter footage of a distinct path of tree damage through a thickly-forested high-elevation area that coincided with a supercell path from June 12, 2022. This area of widespread tree damage was inaccessible and not viewable to the NWS damage survey team that visited the valley nearby immediately following the event.||Post-event interrogation of radar imagery from the event shows a strong rotation couplet above this damage area. After consulting with other Great Plains NWS staff with more than 20 years of tornado-damage-determining experience, this was determined to be tornado damage. The tree fall pattern and path were consistent with strong tornadic rotation. ||The EF2 designation comes from looking at the softwood damage indicator of the Enhanced Fujita Scale. Pictures show thousands of pine trees snapped at various heights, with hardly any trees remaining upright. There was some evidence of debarking in photos as well. For this reason, wind speeds were estimated to be between 128 and 131 mph, based on the upper bound for softwood trunks snapped and the expected damage for softwood debarked. ||Path length and width were determined from polar-orbiting satellite data from the summer months after the event. Notable decreases in vegetation could be seen, with a clearly defined damage path.
Heavy snow fell in the Tetons. Some of the more notable amounts included 20 inches at the Jackson Hole Ski Resort and 17 inches at Grand Targhee Ski Resort.
Snowfall amounts of 6 to 8 inches fell at the base of the Jackson Hole Ski resort, Lesser amounts fell around the town of Jackson.
Numerous SNOTEL sites in the Salt and Wyoming Range reported a foot of new snow.
Snowfall amounts around the foothills of the Star Valley ranged from 5 to 10 inches of snow. Lesser amounts fell around Afton.
Wind gusts as high as 68 mph were reported along Interstate 90. The Johnson County airport near Buffalo had a maximum wind gust of 60 mph.

Very strong winds occurred in the Wind River Mountains. Winds gusted above hurricane force for several hours at Red Canyon along South Pass with a maximum gust of 111 mph. The pass was shut down for several hours due to high wind and blowing snow.
The weather station in Sinks Canyon near Lander reported a maximum wind gust of 65 mph.
Winds gusted as high as 78 mph at the Fales Rock RAWS site. A wind gust to 63 mph was reported near the Pathfinder Reservoir along Highway 220.

There were numerous reports of high winds across Natrona County. The strongest wind gusts were along Wyoming Boulevard south of Casper where a maximum wind gust of 81 mph was reported, Other notable gusts included 65 mph along Hat Six Road and 64 mph at the Natrona County airport.
A maximum wind gust of 81 mph was reported along the Chief Joseph Highway.
A maximum wind gust of 63 mph was reported at the Clark firehouse.
A wind gust of 64 mph was reported at the Sweetwater County airport to the east of Rock Springs. The wind was accompanied by snow which brought very difficult travel conditions along Interstate 80.
A SNOTEL site top west of the eastern entrance of Yellowstone Park reported 14 inches of new snow.
A SNOTEL site to south of the southern entrance to Yellowstone Park reported 19 inches of new snow. Amounts of snow dropped further south.
A combination of snow and blowing snow accompanied by 75 mph wind gusts brought the closure of South Pass over the Wind River Mountains.
A combination of snow and blowing snow accompanied by 75 mph wind gusts brought the closure of South Pass over the Wind River Mountains.
A 59 mph wind gust was reported at the Lander airport.
A 59 mph wind gust was reported at the Natrona County airport to the west of Casper.
Heavy snow fell in the vicinity of Jackson Hole, with a maximum of 20.5 inches at the top of the resort.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Jackson Valley, with a maximum amount of 8 inches at Kelly.
Snowfall amounts in the Star Valley ranged from 6 inches at Afton to 10 inches near Thayne.
The Blind Bull Summit SNOTEL recorded 15 inches of new snow.
High winds occurred in the wind prone areas on the south side of Casper. The maximum wind gust recorded was 67 mph along Wyoming Boulevard.
The wind sensor along the Chief Joseph Highway had sustained winds of 50 mph for an hour and a half with a maximum wind gust of 76 mph.
Heavy snow fell in Yellowstone. Some of the more notable amounts included 16 inches at the Lewis Lake Divide and 16 inches at Two Ocean Plateau.
Snowfall amounts around much of Yellowstone ranged from 12 to 16 inches, including 13 inches at Old Faithful.
Heavy snow fell through the Absarokas, including 13 inches at the Marquette SNOTEL site.
Heavy snow fell throughout the Tetons, including a maximum amount of 26 inches on the summit of the Jackson Hole Ski Resort.
Snowfall amounts in the Jackson Valley ranged from 5 inches in the town of Jackson to 14 inches near Moran Junction.

There were several hours of winds sustained over 50 mph at the Red Canyon wind sensor along South Pass (This stretch of road borders 2 forecast zones). There were many gusts of hurricane force including a maximum gust of 86 mph. The combination of high wind and blowing snow closed Highway 28 for several hours.
The ASOS at the Lander airport reported a maximum wind gust of 66 mph.
High winds occurred in portions of Natrona County. The maximum wind gust was 68 mph along Wyoming Boulevard. Other notable gusts included 64 mph at the Natrona County Airport and along Hat Six Road.
Snow amounts between Thermopolis and Luzerne generally ranged from 6 to 8 inches.
A combination of snow and strong wind caused the closure of the Highway 120 through the Wind River Canyon for several hours.
A combination of strong wind and blowing snow resulted in the closure of Interstate 25 for several hours.

Snowfall amounts in Natrona County ranged from 5 inches at Powder River to 10 inches at Casper to 24 inches in Midwest. The snow was accompanied by strong wind to bring the closure of Interstate 25 and US 20 26 for several hours.
The Casper Mountain SNOTEL measured 12 inches of new snow.
A trained spotter reported 13 inches of snow at Wamsutter. Interstate 80 was closed for many hours by a combination of strong wind an blowing snow.
A combination of snow and gusty wind caused the closure of US 287 for over 48 hours.
A combination of heavy snow and strong wind brought low visibility to South Pass, resulting in the closure of Highway 28.
Most of the area received over 6 inches of snow, including 8 to 11 inches around the city of Riverton.
Snowfall amounts around the Lander foothills generally ranged from 6 to 9 inches.

Temperatures well under 30 below in much of Yellowstone National Park. The lowest temperatures recorded was 45 below zero at Grant Village with the lowest wind chill of 53 below zero at Lake Yellowstone.
Dangerously cold wind chill temperatures occurred in the Absarokas. The coldest wind chill temperatures recorded was minus 61 along Chief Joseph Highway on the evening on December 21st.

Dangerously cold temperatures occurred throughout the Cody Foothills. Wind chills dropped as low as 60 below zero in Cody and minus 50 at the Cody airport on the night of December 21st and 22nd. A period of heavy snow and strong wind followed the Arctic Front Passage resulting in near impossible travel conditions.

Dangerously cold temperatures and wind chills occurred in the Northern Big Horn Basin. The coldest wind chill temperatures recorded were minus 58 at the Powell Airport and minus 55 at the Greybull airport. The towns of Cowley, Basin and Greybull saw low temperatures fall to 35 below zero. A period of snow with winds as high as 64 mph accompanied the passage of the Arctic Front bringing nearly impossible travel conditions.
Bitterly cold wind chill temperatures occurred in the southwestern Bighorn Basin. Kirby was the cold spot with a low temperature of 39 below zero and a wind chill temperature of 48 below zero.

Dangerously cold temperatures and wind chill temperatures occurred in the southeast Big Horn Basin. The low temperature of minus 41 was the 6th coldest temperature ever recorded at the site. The wind chill temperature at the airport dropped to 60 below zero. The Arctic Front was accompanied by a period of snow and wind gusts over 50 mph that brought travel to a standstill for a time.
Temperatures fell as low as 29 below zero with a wind chill down to 50 below zero 10 miles south of Meeteetse.

Extremely cold temperatures occurred in the western Bighorn Range. Temperatures dropped as low as 44 below zero with wind chill temperatures as low as 64 below zero at a WYDOT weather sensor east of Ten Sleep.
Temperatures fell as low as minus 38 in the southeastern Bighorn Mountains with wind chill temperatures as low as 56 below zero to the southwest of Barnum.

Wind chill temperatures under 50 below zero occurred in several locations, including 55 at the Johnson County airport and 57 below near Story.  The lowest air temperature recorded was minus 38 degrees.

Extremely cold temperatures occurred in southern Johnson County. A low of minus 43 was reported southwest of Kaycee with minus 39 reported in town. Wind chill temperatures fell as low as minus 55 along Interstate 25 to the north of Kaycee.
Over a foot of snow fell in portions of the Tetons, with a maximum of 16 inches at the Jackson Hole Ski Resort. High winds in excess of 60 mph also accompanied the snow in the high terrain.

Snowfall amounts in the Jackson Valley ranged from 3 to 10 inches. The snow was accompanied by wind gusts as high as 68 mph at the Jackson Hole Airport which led to almost impossible travel conditions.
Wind chill temperatures fell as low as minus 39 in the western Wind River Mountains.

Wind chill temperatures fell as low as 48 below near in Sinks Canyon State Park with air temperatures as low as minus 29. Strong wind occurred following the Arctic Front passage with wind gusts as high as 86 mph at Red Canyon along South Pass. The wind plus accompanying wind brought very difficult travel conditions including the closure of Wyoming State Route 28 over South Pass.

There were widespread reports of low temperatures below 30 below, including minus 33 at the Dubois airport and minus 38 to the southeast of Dubois. The Arctic Front was accompanied by wind gusts as high as 64 mph and a period of heavy snow that brought travel to a stand still.

The floods were largely confined to low-lying agricultural land and a few dirt roads near the river. This first flood wave from melt in the lower and mid elevations was the highest peak of the season, with peak flow at the Bear River below Pixley Dam gauge reading of 1760 CFS.

Damage to a barn and several outbuildings from a strong thunderstorm wind gust at a ranch between Thermopolis and Kirby WY. Estimated wind gust of 50 to 60 mph based on damage. Damage estimated to have occurred around 426 PM MDT June 4 2023 based on radar. Nearest surface observation was a personal weather sensor 4 miles away, which showed a gust to 22 mph at the 445 pm reporting time, but storm did not directly affect this sensor location. Sheds, items, and debris were blown east to west generally with no indication of distinct rotation. Outbuildings had openings to the east, making them especially susceptible to easterly wind gusts. Little to no damage to nearby farms or trees, as the downdraft was from a small storm, leading to very localized damage, likely from an individual downdraft.

Rainfall reports for the 24 hour period including the flash flood event ranged from 1.30 to 3.47 inches. Flooding was initially reported in downtown Casper where cars where were reported as floating in flowing water. On the south side of Casper, a house was reported as shifted off of its foundation. Interstate 25 became flooded at the peak of the event, and was closed for until well after rainfall ended. Low-lying tunnels on the south side of Casper had as much as 5 feet of water in them at the height of the storm. Damage values have been updated as of Oct 2023 and are from the FEMA presidential disaster declaration, FEMA-4739-DR-WY. No injuries or fatalities were reported to the NWS.

There were numerous reports, pictures, and video of a cone tornado that touched down to the south of Midwest, WY. The tornado remained over open country for the most part. However, the tornado damaged one home where a large section of the roof was removed. Exterior walls remained standing. A trailer was overturned, fuel tanks were blown away, and trees near the residence were damaged.||Based on the FR12 damage indicator category, this tornado was rated EF1 using a low to middle end DOD estimate for the type of construction. Winds are estimated to have been around 110 mph. Stronger winds could have occurred elsewhere along the track, but open country prevented any further evidence of wind damage. Damage survey completed by county emergency management officials.

From Bridger-Teton National Forecast Avalanche Forecast Staff: On January 14, 2024, at approximately 11:30 AM, a skier unintentionally triggered an avalanche on a mid-elevation (8,500���), northwest-facing, sparsely treed slope above an indistinct gully on the Northwest Face of Little Poudre Mountain. This large, soft slab avalanche filled a relatively narrow path. The weak snow layer formed during a prolonged dry period in December that was buried by approximately 30��� of snow falling during a series of storms that began on January 4th. The avalanche broke approximately 50��� wide and 1-3��� deep and entrained more snow along the flanks of a shallow gully. The avalanche fell approximately 600 vertical feet. The slide path is one of several sparsely wooded avalanche paths on the northwest face of Little Poudre Mountain that run the full 1,200��� length of the face. This avalanche was one of the dozens reported in the region during a particularly active avalanche cycle. The skier was killed in the avalanche. No other individuals were injured or killed. Please see avalanche.org for the full event report.

Summary from the USDA FS Bridger Teton Avalanche Center report titled Radio Tower Peak Avalanche Accident: On Saturday, January 4 2025, at approximately 11 am, a group of four skiers unintentionally triggered an avalanche on a north-facing, sparsely treed slope above a steep-walled gully approximately one mile from the parking pullout for Breccia Mountain. The avalanche was remotely triggered from below as the party attempted to cross a gully beneath a wind-loaded ridge. The triggered weak layer was formed during a cold, dry period early in the season. The weak layer was responsible for the region���s numerous human and snowmobile-triggered avalanches the week preceding this accident. This avalanche propagated 350��� uphill to a wind-loaded 38-40 degree slope, broken by cliff bands and across three distinct avalanche paths. The avalanche crown was 400��� across and ranged from one to four feet thick. The debris was a mixture of hard slab and softer surface snow, which slid 625 feet (400 vertical feet) into a terrain trap. The debris carried two members of the group, resulting in one serious injury and one fatality.

On 10/15/25 from 1:35 to 1:37 PM MDT, a thunderstorm produced an EF1 tornado near Alta, WY in the Teton Canyon portion of the Caribou-Targhee National Forest. Reports from social media after the event mentioned tree damage in the Teton Canyon area. Later drone footage taken by the local sheriff's office during the week after this event, as well as satellite imagery, identified a swath of tree damage consistent with 87-104 mph winds (EF1). ||Wind speed was determined using the Enhanced Fujita Scale Damage Indicator for #28 ���Tree - Softwood���, since this tornado occurred in a dense coniferous portion of the Caribou-Targhee National Forest. No structures were in the path. Aerial drone photography showed hundreds of trees blown down by the tornado, with a clear damage swath/path through the forest. A majority of trees in the path were uprooted (Degree of Damage 3, 87 mph) or had their trunks snapped (DoD 4, 104 mph). Bark was visible on trees, and there was no notable debarking or stripping of branches seen in imagery (DoD 5). Given relatively healthy trees with no reason to believe trees were stronger or weaker than average, the lower and upper bounds for the DoDs were not utilized, and expected values were referenced. This led to a wind speed estimate of 87 to 104 mph, which is rated EF1 on the Enhanced Fujita Scale.||The tornado damage path is approximately 1.0 miles long, with a maximum width of 125 yards. The tornado damage path started at an elevation of 7900 ft ASL and ended around 6900 ft.

WYDOT scheduled an avalanche control mission in the early hours of Dec 22 in response to recent weather activity on Wyoming State Highway 22 Teton Pass. Crews remotely detonated avalanche infrastructure in the area known as Glory Bowl and brought down the largest controlled avalanche seen by crews in recent years. A snow slide over 30 feet high and 250 feet wide buried both lanes of travel at milepost 10 on the closed road. Clean up operations lasted about 14 hours and the road was reopened just after 5 PM on Dec 22.

It was a record warm period for much of the latter half of March. The period averaged nearly 15 degrees above normal, with every day but one at least 10 degrees above normal for the daily average temperature. Ten of these days set daily record high temperatures. The previous all time monthly high temperature of 69 was tied or broken six times. This includes four high temperatures in the 70s, which are the first four occurrences on 70 degree temperatures in station history, including the new monthly record high of 73. Records at the Big Piney airport date back to 1998.

The latter half of March featured record warmth for Buffalo. At the Johnson County airport for the period March 17 to 30 every day but one had above normal daily average temperatures, with 10 of those days 10 or more degrees above normal. Five new daily record high temperatures were set. The old monthly record high of 79 degrees was tied or broken four times. There were two high temperatures over 80, which were the earliest occurrences of 80 degrees in station history and the first recorded 80 degree March high temperature in station history. Records at the Buffalo airport date back to 1998.

The latter part of March was a record warm one for Natrona County. The two week period from March 17 to March 30 averaged almost 17 degrees above normal daily average temperatures; with all but two days at least 10 degrees above normal. Nine new daily record high temperatures were set. The old monthly second high temperature of 77 degrees was tied or broken six times, including four days in a row from March 18 to March 21. There were four high temperatures in the 80s, which were the first four occurrences of 80 degrees in March in station history. Records in Casper date back to 1940.

Record warmth occurred over the latter half of March in Big Horn County. The period from March 17 through March 30 averaged more than 12 degrees above normal. Every day but one had above normal daily average temperatures, with ten days more than 10 degrees above normal. Seven new daily record high temperatures were set. The previous monthly record high temperature of 81 was tied or broken on three consecutive days from March 19 to March 21, including a new monthly record high temperature of 85 on March 21. The previous earliest occurrence of 80 degrees was broken by 12 days. Records at the South Big Horn County airport near Greybull date back to 1998.

Most of the second half of March featured record breaking warmth in Yellowstone Park, including at Lake Yellowstone. Daily average temperatures for the period March 17 to March 30 averaged more than 15 degrees above normal. Eight near daily record high temperatures were set. The all time monthly high temperature of 57 degrees was broken on four consecutive days from March 18 to March 21. And, there was the first occurrence of 60 degrees in March in station history on March 19, more than a month earlier than previous earliest occurrence on April 22, 2016. Records at Lake Yellowstone date back to 1998.

The Lander airport experienced record warmth for most of the second half of March. Daily average temperatures from March 17 though March 30 were more than 17 degrees above seasonal normals, with every day above normal. Nine days were more thn 15 degrees above normal. Nine daily record high temperatures were set, including five days in a row from March 17 to March 21. The old monthly high temperature of 76 degrees was broken four times, including three days in a row from March 19 to 21. There were three days of highs in the 80s, the first three in station history. The high of 80 degrees on March 19 was the earliest 80 degree temperature by 22 days. Records at Lander date back to 1892.

It was a record breaking second half of the month of March at the Riverton airport. For the period from March 17 to March 30, the average daily temperatures were more than 17 degrees above normal. For the period March 17 to 21, average temperatures were more than 25 degrees above normal. Eight daily record high temperatures were broken. The previous all time monthly high of 76 degrees was broken 5 times, including four consecutive days from March 18 to 21. There were 3 high temperatures in the 80s, the first three 80 degree high temperatures in March in station history. The high of 80 degrees on March 19 was more than a month earlier than the previous earliest 80 degree of April 22 in 2012. Records at the Riverton airport date back to 1997.

It was a record breaking second half of the month around Rock Springs. At the Sweetwater County airport, average daily temperatures from March 17 through March 30 averaged more than 17 degrees above normal. All but one of those days were more than 11 degrees above normal. Nine new daily record high temperatures were set, including four consecutive days from March 18 to March 21. The previous all time monthly high temperature was tied or broken seven times, with the new all time monthly high of 78 set on March 25. The high of 72 on March 18 was the earliest occurrence of 70 degrees in station history. Records at the Sweetwater County date back to 1948.

Much of the second half of March had record breaking warmth in Washakie County, including at the Worland airport. Average daily temperatures were 13 degrees above normal for the period from March 17 to March 30. During this period, six new daily record high temperatures were set, including on 5 consecutive days from March 17 to March 31. The previous monthly record high temperature of 81 degrees was broken four times, including three consecutive days from March 19 to 21. The high of 80 degrees on March 19 was the earliest occurrence of 80 degrees, breaking the old record of March 28. And finally, the high temperature of 88 degrees on March 21 tied the record high temperature for April.

A lightning strike destroyed or damaged five oil tanks about 20 miles west of Casper near the intersection of county roads 201 and 210. The strike occurred about 1300MST blowing the lid off one tank containing about 400 barrels of crude oil. The fire quickly spread to a nearby tank and burning crude oil ignited the other tanks. Two additional propane tanks were burned but did not explode. A nearly century old storage building at the site was also completely destroyed.

A tornado struck a ranch, including a home, east of Manderson. Three children were in the house at the time of the tornado. The tornado was about 100 feet wide and traveled approximately one-third mile from north-to-south, crossing State Highway 31 before dissipating. Several trees, two fences, and a wooden corral sustained considerable damage. An All-Terrain Vehicle (ATV) was lifted, spun 180 degrees, and moved about 15 feet. A bicycle was tossed onto the roof of the ranch home and several water bins were tossed about.||This landspout tornado occurred in a post-cold frontal environment. A cold front moved through Manderson around 0830MST on Monday leaving northwest wind of 30 to 40 mph in its wake. Solar heating continued to warm the surface while colder air streamed into the region aloft. This helped set the stage for an unstable atmosphere during the afternoon.  A west-moving boundary from showers to the east of Manderson in the Bighorn Mountain foothills helped initiate the updraft that spawned the tornado.

A vicious thunderstorm struck the city of Casper between about 1715 and 1800MST at the start of the July 4th holiday weekend. Extreme rainfall rates falling on the urbanized landscape produced flash flooding throughout Casper, with the most extensive inundation centered around the intersection of Poplar and Collins streets.||Nearly one inch of rain fell in 21 minutes at the Natrona County International Airport northwest of the city. A precipitation gauge along the North Platte River in Casper reported 1.79 inches of rain in 30 minutes. Final tallies around town showed rainfall from around one inch up to a high of about 2.25 inches occurred within about a 35 minute time frame.||Several streets, including Poplar and McKinley were reported to be rivers carrying rocks and other debris toward downtown Casper. Reports indicated one to three feet of water was present on some city streets. The flash flooding floated several cars and sent storm drains shooting wildly into the air. One storm drain cover injured an individual as the surging water displaced it. Emergency management estimated anywhere from 800 to 1000 structures, mainly homes, were impacted by the flooding.||In addition to hundreds of impacted homes, many well known locations also sustained damage, including the Nicolaysen Art Museum, Wyoming Medical Center, Central Wyoming Fairgrounds, Three Crowns Golf Course, and several city school buildings. Major damage also occurred at Casper College where five buildings, including the gymnasium and theater, were significantly impacted. Retaining wall bricks and landscape gravel were washed from a hillside at the college and cascaded to neighboring residences and streets below. The Hall of Justice on North David Street also sustained significant damage when water poured through a door into an underground garage. The building's elevator shafts and the ceilings in several sheriff's offices were also damaged.

The visitors were on walkways and boardwalks surrounding Old Faithful Geyser when the strike occurred around 1430MST. Lightning struck Grand Teton mountain in Grand Teton National Park injuring 17 climbers that were among three separate private climbing parties. One of the injured ultimately fell 2,000 feet to his death as an indirect result of the lightning strike. The climbers were all above 13,000 feet MSL when the lightning storm hit about 1100MST. Helicopters ferried National Park Service rangers to the famed mountain to rescue the injured climbers and search for the body of the deceased. Moderate to severe injuries, ranging from burns to numbness, were suffered by the surviving climbers. The rescue involved the efforts of 83 people.

The snow melted during the previous afternoon and then moved down the river channel during the nighttime hours. Clear Creek crested about 0.2 of a foot above flood stage of 6.0 feet. Heavy snow and cool temperatures in May allowed snowpack to remain at unseasonably high levels across the southern end of the Wind River Range. With over 100 years of weather records, the month of May 2010 ranked as the third coldest at Riverton and tied as the fifth coldest at Lander, both neighboring basin towns. The first warm stretch of the early summer season came on June 2, 3, and 4, as basin temperatures finally climbed into the 70s. In turn, the large snowpack begin a rapid melt that quickly inundated area rivers and streams.||The Middle Fork of the Popo Agie River experienced a rapid rise on Friday afternoon, June 4. The rising waters caused flooding by late evening in the Popo Agie Ranch Estates subdivision south of Lander. Neighbors assisted each other with sandbagging efforts as the water rose through the evening hours. By mid-morning Saturday, June 5, water was causing flooding downstream to the town of Hudson at the confluence of the Middle Fork and Little Popo Agie rivers. Homeowners on the town's west side and farmers and ranchers upstream of Hudson frantically worked to sandbag areas that were not yet inundated by the rapidly rising waters.||Snow continued to melt through the weekend and into Monday, June 7, further exacerbating the flooding. The Mortimore Lane bridge south of Lander was effectively rendered unusable by late morning, June 7. At least five other private bridges in the area were destroyed, as well. Campgrounds in Sinks Canyon State Park were flooded as were Fremont and Third streets in Lander. The Wyoming governor declared all of Fremont County a disaster area on June 7. The Middle Fork of the Popo Agie River near Lander finally crested at 7.50 feet around 2230MST on June 7. This was short of the record of 7.69 feet achieved in June 1963.||As water begin to recede along the Middle Fork, the attention shifted to areas downstream along the Little Wind River. Water levels near the confluence of the Popo Agie and Little Wind rivers around Arapahoe caused 14 homes and several roads to be damaged in that area. A private campground and the historic 1838 Rendezvous site near Riverton were flooded. Farther west along the Little Wind River, the safety of the 17 Mile Road bridge was compromised as the water rose to a record crest. Around 0045MST Wednesday, June 9, the Little Wind River topped out at 11.91 feet, completely shattering the previous record crest of 10.9 feet set in June 1963.||In the end, over 32 square miles of land was impacted by the flood waters, including 38 homes. None of the homes were destroyed. The Wyoming National Guard deployed 400 soldiers to assist in the flood fighting efforts at the peak of the event and over 400,000 sandbags were used. The president declared the county a disaster area on July 14. Public infrastructure damage totaled at least $7.6 million and flood response efforts were estimated at $1.6 million.

Rapid snowmelt runoff and increased water releases from Bull Lake Reservoir caused agricultural flooding along the Wind River around Riverton. Moderate to widespread flooding of agricultural lowlands was reported from Riverton downstream to Black Bridge and on toward Hidden Valley. The river gage on the Wind River at Riverton crested at 9.42 feet at 1045MST on Wednesday, June 9.
The public estimated 60 mph gusts one mile north of the Powder River post office.
The public estimated 70 mph wind gusts five miles east of Powder River.

Lightning struck a haystack at approximately 1525MST on Friday, August 6. The stack, containing 400 tons of premium hay, smoldered for three days before becoming engulfed with flames around 1830MST Monday, August 9. Despite a large response by fire personnel, the entire stack was lost.
Outflow wind of 66 mph was measured along Interstate 25 north of Kaycee.
A severe wind gust associated with thunderstorm outflow was recorded at Snow Springs RAWS.

Damage at a local ranch included a barn roof being ripped off with the remnants scattered across the property. The flying tin roof damaged a corral and injured one horse. Swathed hay that had not yet been baled was completely blown away amounting to a loss of about nine tons.
A peak wind gust of 71 mph was registered by the ASOS at the South Big Horn County Airport just north of Greybull.
The AWOS at Yellowstone Regional Airport recorded a thunderstorm wind gust of 59 mph.

The public reported nickel sized hail two miles east of Buffalo.
A narrow funnel cloud was seen two miles east of Buffalo.

Several reports were received from public sources of a small tornado being viewed looking west from U.S. Highway 310 between Greybull and Lovell.
A thunderstorm moved off the Wind River Mountains over Lander and generated a wind gust of 64 mph at Hunt Field.

The Hot Springs County emergency manager reported penny sized hail along State Highway 120 approximately 23 miles northwest of Thermopolis.

A tornado swept through Juniper trees on a high ridge before descending the hillside into the Nowood River Valley southeast of Ten Sleep. The tornado destroyed several well-built out buildings and downed at least 20, century-old Cottonwood trees on ranches in the valley.
Ping pong ball sized hail fell for several minutes at ranches just west of State Highway 434. Substantial damage was done to the sorghum crop at one ranch.

Ping pong ball sized hail driven by wind gusts estimated to be around 85 mph damaged roofs, rain gutters, windows, and siding of several homes in the Nowood River Valley south of Ten Sleep. The wind also ripped metal roofing from a garage, while another garage was significantly damaged by a toppled Cottonwood tree. A rear flank downdraft associated with a nearby supercell thunderstorm was responsible for the damaging wind.
A funnel cloud which appeared white continued to spin for several minutes after a tornado dissipated.
Hail of one to two inches in diameter fell for 15 minutes just to the south and southeast of Ten Sleep near State Highway 434.
Penny sized hail fell at the Wigwam Fish Rearing Station east of Ten Sleep.
Hail ranging from pea to penny size fell for six minutes about four miles southeast of Cody.
A 63 mph wind gust was recorded at a marina on the west shore of Flaming Gorge Reservoir.
A wind gust to 59 mph was recorded at Ralph Wenz Field southeast of Pinedale.
A thunderstorm moved across the Upper Green River Basin, producing a 64 mph wind gust at Miley Memorial Field airport north of Marbleton.
A strong thunderstorm passed south of Rock Springs and moved through the airport east of town. This storm produced a 76 mph wind gust at the airport.
A strong thunderstorm produced a 76 mph wind gust at the airport east of Rock Springs.
A strong thunderstorm moved northeast across U.S. Highway 20/26 producing quarter sized hail at Natrona.
An off-duty NWS employee and the public each reported two inch diameter hail on Interstate 25 at milepost 195 north of Bar Nunn.
A local television meteorologist submitted a firsthand report of 1.25 inch diameter hail near the Casper/Natrona County International Airport.

A collapsing thunderstorm produced damaging outflow wind. Several large trees and power poles were blown down, especially in the area of Colter Bay and Pilgrim Creek in Grand Teton National Park. Several interior service roads in the park were temporarily blocked by downed trees. Large plate-glass windows were blown out in the Mural Room of Jackson Lake Lodge but no injuries were reported.
Several large trees were blown onto houses causing minor roof damage.

Several ranchers along the Sweetwater River in southern Fremont County reported minor flooding as a result of rapid snowmelt. Much of the flooding occurred around Sweetwater Station. Occasional afternoon and evening showers and thunderstorms added to the rise of the river. Cooler temperatures and a loss of low elevation snow slowed the rising water before the end of May.

Rising temperatures quickly melted low elevation snow in the mountains of extreme eastern Idaho. This caused flooding of Spring, Tin Cup, Crow, Jack Knife, and Stump creeks along the western edge of Star Valley. A few homeowners were forced to sandbag around their homes, build temporary levees, or dig trenches to provide relief from the rising flood waters. These tributaries fed the broad and relatively flat valley of the Salt River. Lowlands near the Salt River were inundated with water, especially north of Thayne to around the Double L Ranch near Etna.

Snowmelt and rainfall combined to raise water levels on the Salt River and its tributaries in Star Valley. A private road and Fairview South Road were partially or completely submerged by flood waters in the vicinity of Fairview. Stump Creek near Auburn and both Crow and Spring creeks near Fairview climbed out of their banks inundating cropland. Along the Salt River, the water was running highest between the communities of Freedom and Etna.

A Memorial Day winter-like storm system brought rain and snow to much of western Wyoming. Runoff from this precipitation event boosted already high water levels on the Blacks Fork River above flood stage. Lowland flooding was reported in the vicinity of Granger and Little America, but no damage to public or private infrastructure occurred. The flooding was most widespread near the confluence of the Hams Fork and Blacks Fork rivers. Sandbagging did take place at the Granger sewer lift pumps and a ranch caretaker's home near the town.

Water levels on the Blacks Fork River retreated below flood stage as snowmelt run-off and rainfall from the previous weekend progressed downstream. Other than lowland flooding, there was no impact to public or private property.

Heavy rain across eastern portions of the Big Horn Basin generated a rapid rise on local rivers. Both the Big Horn and Nowood rivers produced flooding of agricultural lands across southern Big Horn County. Hardest hit areas were in the vicinity of Lane 42 and Lane 50. At least one farmer reported flooding across 25 to 35 acres. The river gauge reached 10.78 feet at Basin, rising over two feet in 24 hours ending Friday morning, June 10. This reading topped the previous record of 10.49 feet back in 1991.
The waters of Tensleep Creek rose rapidly during the early morning hours of Friday, June 24. The basements of several homes east of Ten Sleep were impacted by the flood waters.

Temperatures approaching 70 degrees around 9,500 feet melted snow and caused the water level on Tensleep Creek to quickly rise during the overnight hours of June 29 and 30. The flood waters washed out a road leading to the Wigwam Fish Rearing Station and to a private residence near the mouth of Tensleep Canyon east of town. Several residents also reported flooding of their yards and at least one reported an out-building being inundated by water.

Medicine Lodge Creek rose rapidly during the early morning hours of Friday, June 24 as a result of snowmelt in the western Bighorn Mountains. The rising creek completely flooded the campground area and washed out portions of the main road at Medicine Lodge State Archaeological Site northeast of Hyattville. Water from the creek also ran down State Highway 31 which serves as Main Street in Hyattville. The basement of at least one home was inundated by flood waters from the creek. Officials dug a trench across the highway in Hyattville to relieve flood waters on the upstream side of the road. Flooding of agricultural land also occurred in areas between Hyattville and Manderson along the Nowood River and Medicine Lodge Creek.

Flooding occurred on Shell, Horse, and Trapper creeks as snowmelt runoff increased. Lowland near the creeks and at least one guest ranch were impacted by the rising waters. No bridges were damaged by the high waters but several area roads were inundated and damaged.

Shell Creek and its tributaries caused flooding in and around the community of Shell. The flooding was a result of continued snowmelt in the western Bighorn Mountains as the warmest temperatures of the season were attained. Damage was reported on the Kedesh Guest Ranch and a county road along Trappers Creek.

Medicine Lodge Creek overflowed its banks for the second time in a week causing damage at the Medicine Lodge State Archaeological Site. Much of the site was flooded as waters surged down the narrow creek.

Active snowmelt in the Salt River Range caused a flood along a normally dry ditch in Star Valley Ranch. The narrow drainage near Prater Canyon brought enough water to wash out part of a road and three culverts. The high water also exposed and damaged a water line in the community.

Snowmelt waters traveled down the Greybull River and combined with heavy rain from thunderstorms to create lowland flooding along the river upstream of Greybull. Lane 40 1/2 and Road 5 southwest of Burlington were both inundated by water. The river tried to reroute itself in the vicinity of Road 5. This led county road and bridge employees to construct a new dike to protect one residence and a road.

Flood waters along the Greybull River just upstream of Greybull were responsible for isolating at least two homes as water covered an entire field. The water also inundated low-lying areas along the west side of US Highway 16. The right-of-way fence along the highway was barely showing and nearby barrow pits were almost full.

Melting snow caused the Wind River at Dubois to reach flood stage early on the morning of Friday, June 24. The flood waters surrounded sandbagged homes, inundating yards and a local campground. Continued snowmelt above the 9,000 foot elevation initiated a second surge of water toward the end of the month and early July.||Downstream the river rose several feet as other tributaries brought additional water to the Wind River. Also, increased water releases from the Bureau of Reclamation's Bull Lake Dam, which was quickly filling, allowed for additional water to reach the river channel. The Wind River gauge at Crowheart reached at least 10.86 feet during the early evening of Thursday, June 30, before failing. The Wind River flowed into its old river channel downstream of the Crowheart gauge. This caused water to surround several homes near the U.S. Highway 26 Wind River bridge crossing between Diversion Dam and Morton. Rising water overtopped and subsequently closed a good portion of a one mile section of the highway between mileposts 104 and 105. Traffic was diverted around this closure for most of the next week.||Through late June most of the flooding impacted farm and pasture land near the river from the Johnstown Bridge to Hidden Valley near Boysen Dam. Gauges on this stretch of river at Kinnear and Riverton continued to climb in early July. Similarly, the Little Wind River at Riverton also climbed above flood stage on June 30 and continued to rise during the first few days of July. High waters on tributaries of the Little Wind coupled with record flows on the Wind River created flooding near the confluence with the Wind River.

Flood waters continued to travel down the Wind River through Fremont County in early July. Continued mountain temperatures in the 60s and lower 70s allowed for an unprecedented late-season snowpack to rapidly melt. This active snowmelt quickly filled creeks, streams, and smaller reservoirs feeding the Wind River. The result was record and near record flows on the Wind River from Dubois to Riverton.||The river crested at 5.59 feet in Dubois around 0600MST on Friday, July 1. This was just short of the 5.66 foot record set in June 1956. Flow at the Dubois gauge was calculated at nearly 2,000 cfs. Homes near the river in Dubois were surrounded by water but, other than crawl spaces, no homes were flooded.||Farther downstream at Kinnear the river rose to a record height of 9.69 feet at 0130MST on Saturday, July 2. This reading easily surpassed the previous record of 8.97 feet set in June 1997. Flow on the morning of the 2nd measured 13,586 cfs. Farm and pasture land near the river was completely inundated, in some cases 1/4 to 1/2 mile away from the main channel.||The peak river stage of 11.80 feet occurred on the Wind River at Riverton at 1000MST on July 2. This stage completely shattered by nearly one foot the previous record set in June 1997. Peak flow was measured at 11,759 cfs. Water inundated the Riverton Rendezvous site between Friday and Saturday and disrupted the annual rendezvous. Otherwise, flooding was confined to farm and pasture land, which was particularly pronounced on the east side of Riverton north to Hidden Valley. Flooding of the Little Wind River near the confluence with the Wind River produced much of the same in terms of lowland flooding. The Little Wind River crested just short of 9.0 feet early on July 2, nearly one foot above flood stage. The river fell below flood stage early on Sunday, July 3, following the passage of the Wind River crest wave through Riverton.

Excessive snowmelt runoff caused flooding at Big Horn Lake. The lake elevation hovered about 15 feet above full pool at 3,655 feet. High water neared the level of the US Highway 14A causeway across the southern end of the lake. Wind gusts to 45 mph caused waves that eroded some of the embankment along the causeway and deposited debris onto the highway. On Friday night, July 22, the waves deposited enough debris to necessitate snowplows to come and clear the highway. County Road 20 along the west shore of the lake was inundated and sustained significant damage as a result of the prolonged period of high water.
A thunderstorm moved through central Hot Springs County producing quarter sized hail.

Hail to the size of quarters was reported at the Canyon Visitor Center. Nearby roadways were covered with two to three inches of hail of varying size.
ASOS registered a 60 mph wind gust at Casper/Natrona County International Airport.

Nickel sized hail fell at a ranch along the Lower Greybull River Road northeast of Meeteetse.
One inch diameter hail dented vehicles, broke a few windows, and punched holes in the siding of some homes around Grover.

The New Fork River was flooded in sections around State Highway 351 and upstream near the confluence of Boulder Creek.

Horse Creek and other small tributaries of the Green River near Daniel overflowed their banks quickly flooding lowlands and nearly impacting several roads. The flood waters caused several homes north and east of Daniel to be sandbagged around their perimeter.
High water on the Green River near LaBarge above Fontenelle Reservoir caused the inundation of County Road 318 and lowland areas in the broad river plain.
A trained spotter reported a large tree snapped by a thunderstorm wind gust. The tree fell on a shed, causing significant damage to the roof and moving it slightly off its foundation.
Two power poles were felled by a wind gust associated with outflow from a thunderstorm.

A 48-year-old woman was killed when her light truck rolled four times north of Shoshoni near milepost 105.6 on U.S. Highway 20. Several other accidents were reported including a three car pileup that sent three people to the hospital with non-life threatening injuries.
A trained spotter reported quarter sized hail at a ranch southeast of Ten Sleep.

Lightning injured a 25-year-old man when it struck next to him as he was helping set a manufactured home north of Lander. The man was on his hands and knees on wet ground when the bolt struck near him and traveled through his body around 1300MST. The bolt exited his back leaving a large blister and he was hospitalized for three days as a result. After returning home the man was still experiencing chest pain, blurry eyesight, and pain in his extremities.
A high-based thunderstorm moved along Interstate 80 producing a severe wind gust at a sensor near Bitter Creek.

A thunderstorm rolled across the northern Big Horn Basin and produced a severe wind gust at an automated station in Powell.

Thunderstorm outflow produced a 64 mph wind gust at Worland Municipal Airport.

A microburst associated with a strong thunderstorm that developed near Rafter J Ranch and swept north caused widespread tree and property damage. Most of the damage was concentrated in Jackson and in a swath from south of town to the northwest of town toward Teton Village. Dozens of uprooted trees caused minor roof damage and a carport collapsed at Jackson Hole Lodge in Jackson.

An isolated thunderstorm formed west of Casper and tracked along the south side of town. The storm produced a microburst that blew out car windows and caused damage to about 20 vehicles at Casper Country Club. The wind also snapped a 70-foot-tall tree at the golf course and damaged a tall chain link fence surrounding the tennis courts.
An automated sensor at Crowheart recorded a thunderstorm wind gust of 81 mph. The storm damaged several healthy trees, snapping off six to eight inch diameter limbs.
Strong wind snapped healthy tree branches up to two inches in diameter in the town of Pavillion.
Many healthy tree branches up to three inches in diameter were snapped off by strong wind at a home north of Kinnear.
A strong thunderstorm produced wind that snapped healthy branches two to three inches in diameter off trees north of Fort Washakie.

A strong thunderstorm formed west of Riverton and produced a wind gust of 67 mph at Riverton Regional Airport.

A strong thunderstorm produced a 58 mph wind gust at a remote observing station.

A thunderstorm moved across the southern Absaroka Range and sent strong outflow wind southeast across the western Owl Creek Mountains.  A remote weather station recorded a peak wind gust of 64 mph.
A 73 mph wind gust was reported in association with a thunderstorm eight miles west of Thermopolis. The gust was recorded at a residence with an automated weather station.
A strong thunderstorm produced a 59 mph wind gust at an automated weather station on Boysen Peak.
A severe thunderstorm produced damaging wind at a local golf course and at the home of an NWS employee.
A strong thunderstorm moved east of the Absaroka Mountains and produced a severe wind gust at an automated observing site along State Highway 120 north of Meeteetse.
A strong thunderstorm moved off the Absaroka Range and produced a severe wind gust of 60 mph at the Grass Creek Divide RAWS site.
A strong thunderstorm brought a severe wind gust of 58 mph to the Pinedale Airport.
An individual with an automated wind sensor reported a thunderstorm wind gust of 72 mph.
Strong wind gusts of 78 and 77 mph were reported at Chief Joseph.
A wind gust to 59 mph was recorded at an automated station on the west side of Cody. In addition, winds were sustained at 42 mph at Meeteetse with gusts to 58 mph.
The North Zone RAWS site reported a wind gust of 113 mph at an elevation of 10750 feet.
A wind gust of 75 mph was reported at the Riverton Airport. A National Weather Service employee also reported a wind gust of 62 mph at 1527LST at the Riverton Country Club.

High winds blew for several hours across the lower elevations of Natrona County. The WYDOT weather sensor at Highland reported sustained winds as high as 52 mph with gusts as high as 76 mph.  The Casper Airport reported a wind gust to 60 mph.

The Buckboard Marina reported a wind gust to 65 mph.

Winds were sustained at 40-45 mph at Shute Creek.
Winds over 50 mph and snow produced white out conditions.
Winds gusts of 63 mph combined with snow produced white-out conditions over South Pass.
Sustained winds of over 40 mph were reported at both Continental Divide and Tipton.
Winds gusted to 65 mph a Fales Rock and 63 mph at Beaver Rim.
Wind gusts of 58 mph were reported at Hiland.

There were numerous reports of heavy snow throughout Natrona County. The city of Casper received anywhere from 6 to 14 inches, 12 inches was reported at Evansville, 10 inches at Mills and 9 inches at Bar Nunn.
Trained spotters and SNOTEL stations reported 16 to 18 inches of snow.
There were numerous reports of heavy snow across the Wind River Basin. Snowfall amounts ranged from 5 inches in Shoshoni to 10 to 12 inches in Riverton and Hudson.
A trained spotter reported 21 inches of snow at Sinks Canyon State Park. The Townsend Creek SNOTEL station estimated 26 inches of snow.
Numerous reports of over 18 inches of snow were reported in the Lander Foothills; including a maximum of 27 inches.

Many locations reported wind gusts of over 60 mph. In Green River, there were numerous reports of damage. Many trees were blown down and some fences were damaged. A large window was blown in at the Aquatic Center at Western Wyoming Community College in Rock Springs, where 1,200 customers lost power when a power pole was damaged.
A COOP Observer reported damage to a couple of docks at the Buckboard Marina.
A trained spotter reported 7 inches of snow at Wamsetter. Drifts as high as 3 and a half feet were reported. A maximum gust of 71 mph was recorded at the Rock Springs Airport.
A trained spotter at Jeffrey City reported 12 inches of snow. In addition, State Highway 287 was closed from Lander to Muddy Gap for several hours.
There were several reports of 6 to 16 inches of snow around Thermopolis.
Numerous reports of 6 to 11 inches of snow in Riverton were received. 8 inches of snow was reported at Hudson.
Heavy snow fell across the eastern slopes of the Wind River Mountains. 18 inches of snow was reported at the St. Lawrence Alt SNOTEL.
A storm total of 13.2 inches was measured at the Lander airport. 8 to 14 inches was measured around the city of Lander with over 20 inches in some of the outlying areas.
A trained spotter reported 7 inches of snow in Jeffrey City.

Heavy snow fell across much of the lower elevations of Natrona County. Snowfall amounts ranged from 12 inches in Mills, up to 16 inches in Casper with up to 2 feet in southern portions of Casper bordering Casper Mountain.
Very heavy snow fell on Casper Mountain. The Reno Hill SNOTEL estimated 29 inches of snow. Spotter reports ranged from 3 feet to as much as 56 inches.

A wind gust of 82 mph was reported 5 miles west northwest of Clark. Around 5 miles southeast of Meeteetse, a tractor trailer was blown over. The driver was injured and transported to the hospital. Liquid fertilizer and some diesel fuel were spilled from the truck.
The Lander airport recorded 13.1 inches of snow from the evening of April 30 through May 1.
A spotter reported 12 inches of snow at Big Piney. 11 inches of snow was measured at Marbleton.
Wind gusts of 60 and 62 mph were reported at the Riverton Regional Airport ASOS from the gust front ahead of a line of thunderstorms.
A trained spotter reported hail the size of quarters covering the ground.
A trained spotter reported several funnel clouds as well as a rotating wall cloud north of Worland.

Heavy rain from thunderstorms brought flash flooding to the Medicine Lodge State Archaeological Site. Debris covered the main road leading into the park in several spots, occasionally to a depth of one to two feet. At least six campsites in the park were damaged when normally dry arroyos to the east of the park swept water and debris across them before emptying into Medicine Lodge Creek.
