Heavy rain of the previous week had filled the Big Horn River and the snowmelt run-off in the Greybull River began to back-up near the confluence. A small levee was reported to have collapsed upstream of the confluence causing further problems. Sandbags were deployed to prevent damage. Most of the flooding was confined to low-lying areas and little damage was reported.

Rapid snowmelt in the Wind River Range caused the Wind River near Dubois to rise slightly above flood stage. The river upstream of Dubois crested at 5.01 feet during the morning of Tuesday, June 2. The flooding was confined to lowlands near the river and caused no damage.

Minor flooding occurred along the Wind River near Riverton. The river crested to 9.12 feet at 0345MST on Wednesday, June 3. Heavy rain of the previous week and increased snowmelt run-off combined to cause the high water. The flooding only impacted lowlands nearest the river on the south side of Riverton.
Ping pong ball sized hail was observed by a trained spotter near the intersection of US Highway 20/26 and Bucknum Road west of Casper.
Hail of various sizes fell in Midwest, with the largest stones being one inch in diameter. Most of the stones were penny and nickel sized.
Hail as large as one inch in diameter fell in Shoshoni.

Strong thunderstorms produced heavy rain across eastern Johnson and western Campbell counties near Interstate 90. The heaviest rain, estimated at three inches, fed Dead Horse Creek, a small tributary of the Powder River. Dead Horse Creek overflowed and eventually inundated a stretch of Interstate 90 around mileposts 90 and 91, which resulted in the closure of the road from late Wednesday evening, June 3, until the morning of June 4.

The last in a series of thunderstorms on Wednesday, June 3, brought very heavy rain to Buffalo and the surrounding area. The ASOS at Johnson County Airport measured 0.98 inches of rain in less than 25 minutes as the storm moved north and then stalled over Buffalo. The ASOS recorded a grand total of 1.26 inches in less than one hour. Saturated soils were unable to absorb the rain which quickly ran through the streets of Buffalo and filled area creeks. Five Buffalo homes were declared destroyed, and the senior center and BLM office sustained flood damage. Some reports indicated water four feet deep in low-lying areas. The water was running fast enough to lift and carry the top layer of pavement on a couple of Buffalo streets. A few county roads and some private bridges were washed out due to culvert failures as a result of the raging flood waters.
The Hot Springs County Emergency Manager reported nickel sized hail along State Highway 431 just east of State Highway 120 toward Gooseberry Creek.

Ping pong ball sized hail fell at Midvale. The storm continued to move northeast and impact areas along North Portal Road, which was covered to a depth of three inches with hailstones of various sizes.

Slow-moving thunderstorms brought very heavy rain to areas west of Casper and led to flash flooding in several areas. The greatest impact was felt on US Highway 20/26 which was flooded in several locations and had to be closed between Casper and Shoshoni for several hours. The worst of the flooding was between mileposts 15 and 19 around Emerald Acres subdivision. Other flooding also occurred around Bucknum Road and 10 Mile Road. Portions of Poison Spider Road were also flooded and one home was surrounded by water.
The cooperative observer southwest of Meeteetse reported hail of various sizes with a few stones the size of quarters.

The superintendent at Medicine Lodge State Archaeological Site reported flooding of three dry arroyos in and south of the park. One arroyo flooded campsites in the middle campground and flooding of other arroyos covered sections of the last one-half mile of a road leading to the park.
An off-duty NWS Meteorologist reported penny sized hail covering Gas Hills Road to a depth of one inch.
The public posted a picture on Facebook of half dollar sized hail in Ethete.

The Wind River gauge near Riverton was above flood stage for over a week because of run-off from melting snow and recent rainfall. Water levels fluctuated each day with the daily peak occurring during the early to mid morning hours. The river crested at 10.27 feet at 0700MST on Friday, June 12.

The river gauge on the South Fork of the Shoshone River near Valley reached or topped flood stage three separate times due to diurnal fluctuations between the evening of June 8 and the morning of June 13. Water levels typically peaked around midnight with a crest of 8.43 feet at 0015MST on Thursday, June 11.

Slow-moving showers and thunderstorms dropped heavy rain in a small drainage basin west of Medicine Lodge State Archaeological Site. Run-off in the basin fed a dry wash that brought water into the central portion of the park. The dry wash directed water into and around a newly refurbished small cabin that serves as a visitor center. There was minor damage to the park road.
Golf ball sized hail was reported at a pair of rural ranches along Tipperary Road east of Buffalo. The hail caused body damage to some vehicles.
Hail up to the size of pennies was reported by trained spotters north of Shell.
Trained spotters and law enforcement reported penny sized hail in Lander. Law enforcement also reported that a few stones were the size of quarters.
Hail up to the size of pennies fell in a swath from west of Riverton, to the NWS office, to about five miles north of town.
A NWS Employee found penny sized hail two inches deep 15 minutes after a storm passed across State Highway 135 near Sand Draw.
Trained spotters reported hail ranging in size from quarters to golf balls at Star Valley Ranch.
The Lincoln County Sheriff's Office reported quarter sized hail covering roads in Afton. A trained spotter also reported one inch diameter hail just to the northwest of town.
Two inch diameter hail fell in the Wind River Canyon knocking out windows in vehicles traveling State Highway 789.
The Natrona County emergency manager reported hail up to the size of ping pong balls near the intersection of state highways 220 and 487.
The gauge on the Wind River near Riverton briefly crested at 9.10 feet at 2330MST on Wednesday, June 17. No damage was reported as the flooding only impacted bottomland nearest the river.
Golf ball sized hail fell at a ranch along Tipperary Road east of Buffalo. The hail broke one window at a home on the ranch.
The wind sensor along State Highway 120 on Meeteetse Rim recorded a thunderstorm wind gust to 63 mph.
A trained spotter reported one inch diameter hail approximately nine miles east of Evansville near the Converse County line.
A rancher along the Greybull River northeast of Meeteetse reported one inch diameter hail.
Trained spotters reported quarter to golf ball sized hail just east of State Highway 120 near the Gooseberry Creek Rest Stop.

Heavy rain fell in the tributaries of the Powder River in southern Johnson and northern Natrona counties. The South Fork of the Powder River along with Salt Creek were two of the major contributors to a rapid rise in the water level of the Powder River near Sussex. High water on both the North and Middle forks of the Powder River also served to flood the main stem. The river climbed more than 10 feet in less than 24 hours at Sussex and crested at 15.63 feet around 0500MST on Monday, May 25. This crest topped the previous record crest of 15.16 feet set in May 1978. Agricultural land downstream of Kaycee near Sussex was completely inundated and several ranches and vehicles were surrounded by water.

Heavy rain of one-half to one inch inundated dry washes and arroyos in and around Medicine Lodge State Archaeological Site. Water and mud flowing out of one small canyon caused damage to at least six campsites in the middle portion of the site.

A thunderstorm rapidly developed to the south of Cody and tracked north over the city producing heavy rain and copious amounts of small hail. Hail drifts were measured in feet in some areas with a few low spots accumulating close to six feet of hail. The hail prevented the heavy rain from draining easily and water accumulated on area roads. Several business owners in downtown Cody reported minor flooding as the water piled up in the streets, especially along Sheridan Avenue. A bakery had water on the floors and in the basement and a gift shop flooded.

Heavy rain fell across southern Johnson County and brought flooding to the tributaries of the North Fork and Middle Fork of the Powder River. Flooding was observed between Mayoworth and Kaycee and also between Barnum and Kaycee.

Heavy rainfall led to flooding in Lyons Valley near Lander. The Little Popo Agie River overflowed its banks and flooded low lying areas along Lyons Valley Road. The water approached some homes along the river but did not enter them.

A flood wave moved north down the Powder River as a result of heavy rain over the Memorial Day Weekend. For the most part, impacts were confined to low lying land nearest the river. However, there was flooding of some infrastructure near the Interstate 90 Powder River bridge in eastern Johnson County.
Snowfall of 12 inches was estimated at the Townsend Creek SNOTEL.

The Rock Springs Police Department reported flooding in a trailer park on 9th Street near the South Side Belt Route. Up to 3 feet of water collected in low-lying areas of the park and displaced some residents before the water receded shortly after 2100MST. Several media outlets shared pictures of street flooding in and around downtown Rock Springs.

A second straight day of drenching thunderstorms brought widespread flash flooding throughout the city of Rock Springs. Many businesses and residential basements were flooded. In addition, numerous cars were stranded in flood waters both on city streets and in large parking lots.
The ASOS at the Rock Springs-Sweetwater County Airport registered a thunderstorm wind gust of 64 mph.

A light residential trailer was blown over and knocked into a car on the north side of Rock Springs. The strong wind also dropped large tree limbs and caused damage to a power pole in downtown Rock Springs.
Quarter sized hail was reported in Burlington.
Weak convection and a strong pressure gradient combined to produce a peak wind gust of 76 mph shortly before 1500MST at the Split Rock Creek RAWS.

Several wind gusts over 58 mph were recorded at Thermopolis with a peak speed of 67 mph. The gusts were the result of weak convection and a strong pressure gradient ahead of an approaching cold front.
Weak convection coupled with a tight pressure gradient combined to produce wind gusts of 59 and 62 mph at the Casper-Natrona County International Airport.
Dime to quarter sized hail was reported at a ranch between Barnum and Kaycee.
A spotter just west of I-25 near the Johnson-Natrona County line reported one inch diameter hail.
Hailstones as large as ping pong balls fell in Edgerton. Most of the stones ranged in size from a dime to a quarter.
An automated anemometer recorded a thunderstorm outflow wind of 60 mph in Midwest.
A trained spotter reported a funnel cloud between Kaycee and Sussex.
Quarter sized hail fell near Missouri Flat Road west-northwest of Thermopolis.
Hail up to the size of nickels was reported about five miles north of Lysite.
A funnel cloud was observed and photographed east of Lost Cabin.
One inch diameter hail fell at a ranch in rural Johnson County north of Interstate 90. The hail was part of an at least 10 mile swath of large hail that moved east across the county.
Motorists on US Highway 20/26 were forced to pull over due to nickel sized hail and heavy rain reducing visibility.
One in a series of strong thunderstorms dropped penny sized hail near Buffalo.

Small tributaries feeding Salt Creek in southeast Johnson County were out of their banks as a result of an estimated three inches of rainfall on already saturated soils. Additional water upstream near Midwest, where 1.07 inches of rain fell in 30 minutes late Wednesday, June 3, moved downstream and exacerbated the rural flooding. The extreme run-off eventually caused rises of over one foot per hour on the much wider Powder River at Sussex.
Hail up to the size of golf balls was reported near Emblem.

Westerly pre-frontal winds ahead of an approaching cold front reached 59 mph at Riverton Regional Airport. Numerous limbs were downed around Riverton. Two trees were also toppled in town with one falling on a power line.

A tornado was witnessed just north of Interstate 80 between Tipton and Red Desert Roads to the west of Wamsutter. The touchdown was very brief and the tornado remained over open country producing no damage.

The AWOS at the North Big Horn County Airport near Cowley had several wind gusts in excess of 60 mph between 1455 and 1555MST. The wind was primarily from the northwest with the strongest gust being 63 mph at 1455MST. The wind gusts were the result of weak convection combining with already gusty surface wind associated with a cold frontal passage.
Wind gusts associated with a strong cold front and weak convection reached 74 mph at the South Big Horn County Airport just north of Greybull.
The wind gusted to 59 mph at Johnson County Airport in Buffalo.
A gust to 59 mph was measured at Riverton Regional Airport.
The ASOS at Casper-Natrona County International Airport reported a wind gust to 60 mph.

Strong north wind in the wake of a cold front struck a storage unit oriented west-to-east on the north side of the North Platte River. The nearly perpendicular wind eventually tore a portion of the roof and walls from the unit and threw the debris over 100 feet into the river.
The ASOS at the Hunt Field reported a wind gust to 58 mph.
A wind gust to 60 mph was measured by the ASOS at the Rock Springs-Sweetwater County Airport.
The RAWS site at Fales Rock recorded a wind gust of 58 mph.
The sensor at Hiland recorded wind gusts of 63 mph.
The wind sensor along Chief Joseph reported several wind gusts past 74 mph including a maximum of 80 mph.
A wind sensor 5 miles west-northwest of Clark reported a wind gust to 64 mph.
The RAWS sensors at Camp Creek and Fales Rock recorded wind gusts of 61 and 65 mph, respectively. Another anemometer on Beaver Rim measured a 60 mph gust around 1000MST.
The wind sensor at Twenty Mile Hill recorded a wind gust to 58 mph. The WYDOT anemometer on Wyoming Boulevard on the south side of Casper measured a gust to 65 mph at 0841MST.
Wind gusts along State Highway 28 between Lander and the top of Red Canyon routinely gusted over 60 mph for several hours.
The Crooked Creek Wildfire blew up in the early afternoon of Monday, September 28, and consumed 359 acres by the end of September.
Numerous wind gusts past 58 mph were recorded near Clark including peak speeds of 76 and 89 mph.
Winds were sustained at over 40 mph with gusts to 58 mph in Cody.
The wind prone areas near Clark had several wind gusts past 58 mph. The maximum wind gust was 88 mph to the west of Clark at 0215MST.
A wind gust of 61 mph was recorded at Tipton. Other strong wind gusts included 60 mph at Continental Divide and 59 mph at the Rock Springs airport.
The RAWS site at Fales Rock recorded several wind gusts past 58 mph including a maximum of 68 mph. A wind gust of 60 mph was recorded at Camp Creek.
The wind sensor at Hiland recorded wind gusts of 58 mph.
The ASOS at Hunt Field in Lander recorded a wind gust to 59 mph.
An avalanche on Teton Pass buried two snowmobilers under up to five feet of snow. One of the skiers suffered a broken leg.

West-northwest moving showers and thunderstorms tracked up the south slope of the Bighorn Mountains during the late afternoon of October 2. Heavy rain estimated at 0.75 inch to around 1.00 inch fell in a 20 to 30 minute period in the Buffalo Creek drainage. The water quickly ran off the steep slopes into creeks and streams feeding Buffalo Creek. Eyewitness reports indicated the creek went from a dry creek to well outside its banks in just minutes. The raging waters damaged a county road in several spots, overtopped and damaged a ranch road, and ruined fence line at a rural ranch.
The Lander Hunt Field ASOS recorded a peak wind to 59 mph.
Very strong wind gusts occurred in the favored areas near Clark. There were many gusts of hurricane force recorded including a maximum of 104 mph around 0100MST.
A wind gust of 59 mph was recorded at the Dubois Airport with a peak gust of 58 mph at Crowheart.
A WYDOT wind sensor on the west side of Rock Springs recorded a wind gust of 65 mph. The sensor at Peru Hill along Interstate 80 had a gust of 59 mph.
Wind gusts over 58 mph were recorded at numerous sites across eastern Sweetwater County. The maximum gust was 68 mph at Rock Springs-Sweetwater County Airport at 1127MST.
Several sites across northern Johnson County recorded wind gusts over 58 mph. Some of the strongest gusts included 84 mph at Indian Creek and 74 mph at the Buffalo Airport.
The ASOS at Riverton Regional Airport recorded a wind gust of 60 mph. A wind gust of 62 mph was recorded northwest of Hudson at the Sharpnose RAWS.
The weather sensor on Outer Drive in Casper reported several wind gusts above 58 mph including a maximum of 68 mph around 0350MST.
A wind gust of 60 mph was recorded at North Big Horn County Airport in Cowley. The ASOS at the South Big Horn County Airport in Greybull registered a wind gust of 58 mph.
Thr RAWS site at Camp Creek recorded several hours of wind gusts over 58 mph including a maximum of 81 mph. The site at Fales Rock had a maximum gust of 68 mph.
Moderate to heavy snow fell across Natrona County. The heaviest snow occurred in areas closer to Casper Mountain and southwest of Casper. Amounts of around 6 to 8 inches were common in this area.
Heavy snow fell across much of the region. The highest amount measured was 9 inches at Jeffrey City.
Heavy snow fell throughout the Lander Foothills. Widespread amounts of 10 to 12 inches were recorded including 11.4 inches at the Lander Airport.
Heavy snow fell across the Wind River Basin. Amounts ranged from 6 inches at Shoshoni to 9.6 inches at the Riverton Airport.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Wind River Mountains above Lander. Snowfall at Homestead Park was measured at more than a foot with the bulk of the snow occurring on Wednesday, November 25.
The wind sensor 5 miles west-northwest of Clark recorded wind gusts of 81 and 76 mph.
The RAWS site at Fales Rock recorded several wind gusts over 58 mph including a maximum of 68 mph.
Several wind gusts over 58 mph were recorded on Outer Drive north of Casper, including a maximum gust of 70 mph.
The wind sensor along the North Fork of the Popo Agie river recorded wind gusts of 58 and 59 mph.
Strong winds occurred along the Chief Joseph highway. Winds were sustained as high as 73 mph. Many gusts over hurricane force were recorded, including a maximum of 96 mph.
The wind sensor along the Chief Joseph Highway recorded sustained winds of 60 mph with many gusts of hurricane force. The maximum wind gust was 96 mph.
Hurricane force wind gusts occurred at all three wind sensors in the vicinity of Clark. The strongest gusts were 103 mph 5 miles WNW of Clark, 80 mph 8 miles SSW of Clark, and 74 mph at Clark.

Widespread heavy rain of 2.50 to 4.50 fell in a broad swath across Fremont County during a 48-hour period from Friday evening, May 6, through Sunday evening, May 8. There was a peak rainfall amount of 6.88��� at a rain gauge about 6 miles west of Fort Washakie on the Little Wind River. The heavy rain fell over the lower elevations of the Wind River Basin and in the lower foothills of the Wind River Range.||The heaviest rainfall occurred between 1900MST Friday, May 6, and 1700MST Saturday, May 7. The rain gauge at Lander Hunt Field reported 3.82��� in this 22-hour period, with 1.12��� falling between 0800MST and 1100MST Saturday. The heavy rainfall contributed to significant rises along the Little Wind River and its tributaries, particularly the Little Popo Agie River through Lyons Valley. The rapid river rises produced substantial flooding from Lyons Valley, to Hudson, to Arapahoe.||Overland flow was a significant contributor to the rapidly rising rivers. Recent rains had left soils relatively wet, so as rainfall piled up on Saturday morning water began to flow across fields, overwhelm ditches, and fill ravines. These waters made their way to the larger rivers and quickly filled them. By early Saturday afternoon, there were reports of water covering low-lying areas of roads north and northwest of Lander. The rain was so heavy that water seeped through the walls at the hospital in Lander prompting the evacuation of patients. Some basement flooding was reported in residential areas of Lander. By mid-afternoon Saturday, reports were received of flood waters on the Little Popo Agie River surrounding homes in Lyons Valley. Several rural roads were either covered with water or damaged by the flood waters in the valley. The flood waters on this tributary combined with the already high water on the Popo Agie River to cause water levels to surge in Hudson late Saturday evening and early Sunday morning. The subsequent flooding damaged or destroyed several mobile homes along the river on the west side of Hudson. Sunday afternoon saw the retreat of water levels on these rivers with a subsequent decrease in flood-related problems.||Multiple tributaries and overland flow to small creeks, streams, and ditches quickly filled the Little Wind River near Arapahoe downstream to around Riverton. The river topped flood stage of 8 feet at 0605MST Sunday, May 8, and climbed about 1 foot every three to four hours during the morning and early afternoon. The  river crested at 10.19 feet between 1545MST and 1600MST Sunday as residents along the river scrambled to fill sandbags and move property to a safer location. Flood waters on the Little Wind River retreated slowly on Monday, May 9, before falling below flood stage at 0120MST on Tuesday, May 10. The river fell below action stage by the end of Tuesday.

The strong winds blew over a tractor trailer truck along Outer Drive south of Casper, resulting in the closure of the road for several hours. The strong winds also knocked out power to close to 5000 people in Casper when the winds were strongest.

Very strong winds occurred in the wind prone areas around Clark including a maximum wind gust of 108 mph. Gusts over 58 mph also occurred near Cody and in Powell. The prolonged period of strong wind caused extensive blowing and drifting of the deep snow pack on the ground. As a result, many roads became impassable and many motorists were stranded. Some residents in outlying areas were stranded for days before roads could be cleared after the wind subsided.
The RAWS site at Fales Rock recorded several wind gusts exceeding 58 mph. including a maximum of 68 mph.
The WYDOT site along Outer Drive south of Casper recorded several wind gusts exceeding 58 mph. including a maximum of 68 mph.
Heavy snow fell in the Jackson Valley. Snowfall amounts ranged from 4 inches at Alta to 15 inches around Wilson.

Heavy bands of snow set up across the central Wind River basin and produced heavy amounts of snow. Amounts around Riverton generally ranged from 7 to almost 10 inches. The 7.8 inches measured at downtown Riverton made it the snowiest Christmas Day on record.
A spotter measured 7 inches of snow in Thermopolis.
There are numerous reports of 7 to 10 inches of new snow around the city of Worland.

Across southern Natrona County, anywhere from 7 to 11 inches of new snow fell. The snow combined with a strong wind at times to bring very difficult travel conditions that caused the closure of Interstate 25 for a time.

Winds increased rapidly across northern Johnson County and combined with heavy snow to produce a prolonged period of blizzard conditions. Visibility was down to near zero at times and prompted the closure of Interstate 90 for several hours.
The Grassy Lake SNOTEL reported 14 inches of snow. On top of the Jackson Hole Ski Resort, 12 inches of new snow was measured.
High winds occurred through the Cody Foothills. The highest winds were around Clark, where winds gusted as high as 96 mph. A gust to 59 mph was recorded on the west side of Cody.
The RAWS site at Fales Rock had several wind gusts over 58 mph, including a maximum of 83 mph. Some other notable gusts included 74 mph at Camp Creek and 61 mph at Jeffrey City.

Hurricane force winds occurred in Casper and caused significant damage. Wind gusts of 88 mph were clocked along Outer Drive with 64 mph at the Casper airport. Damage around Casper included several car ports being destroyed at the Pheasant Ridge Apartment Complex that damaged several cars, a tree falling on two trucks along CY Avenue and a trailer blowing over at the Sunrise Shopping Center.

A snowboarder was walking on a cornice that failed and triggered an avalanche below him. The snowboarder was swept over a large cliff and buried in an area called Beards Wheat Field. He was found by a search dog after avalanche hazard work with explosives was performed.
There were many wind gusts past hurricane force near Clark. The strongest gusts included 99 mph 5 miles west-northwest of Clark and 78 mph 8 miles south of Clark.
The RAWS site at Fales Rock had a maximum wind gust of 61 mph.
Strong winds occurred once again along Outer Drive south of Casper. There were many gusts past 58 mph with a maximum of 78 mph.
Heavy snow fell through much of the Star Valley. Some totals included 11 inches in Afton and 13 inches in Alpine.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Salt and Wyoming Range. Some of the higher totals included 17 inches at Commissary Ridge and 14 inches at the Hams Fork SNOTEL.
At Fossil Butte, eight inches of new snow was measured.
A CocoRaHS observer measured 6 inches of new snow 5 miles north of Farson.
New snowfall amounts of 6 to 10 inches were common across Green River and Rock Springs, including 11.4 inches 4 miles NNW of Rock Springs.
The CoCoRaHS observer at Buckboard Marina measured 8 inches of new snow.
A trained spotter measured 6 inches of new snow at Wamsutter.
A trained spotter reported 7.4 inches of snow at Daniel.
Frigid temperatures occurred in Yellowstone Park. Some of the low temperatures included minus 41 degrees at the Lamar Ranger Station and -35 degrees at the northeast entrance to Yellowstone Park.
The temperature dropped to minus 30 degrees at Greybull.
A weather station 9 miles northeast of Thermopolis recorded a low temperatures of minus 33 degrees.
The COOP observer at Kaycee recorded a low temperature of minus 30 degrees.
Frigid temperatures occurred throughout the Jackson Valley. Some of the coldest lows included minus 36 degrees at the Jackson Hole Airport and minus 32 degrees at Moose.

Brutally cold temperatures occurred on the morning of January 6th. Some of the coldest lows included minus 38 degrees, two miles south of Riverton, minus 33 degrees at the COOP observer and minus 32 degrees at Hudson.
A trained spotter reported a low temperature of minus 31 degrees at Lander.
The COOP observer reported a low temperature of minus 33 degrees at Jeffrey City.
A weather sensor at Independence Rock recorded a low temperature of minus 41 degrees.
Very cold temperatures occurred through the Star Valley. Among the coldest temperatures recorded was minus 35 degrees at the Afton airport.
Frigid temperatures occurred throughout the region. Some of the coldest temperatures included minus 44 degrees at Bondurant and minus 36 degrees at the Pinedale airport.
Extreme cold occurred through the Upper Green River Basin, including minus 32 degrees at the Farson COOP.
Frigid temperatures were common across Southern Lincoln County. Some of the lowest temperatures included minus 40 degrees south of Cokeville and minus 32 degrees at Kemmerer.
Temperatures of minus 30 or below were commonplace across the region, including minus 35 degrees, three miles northwest of Rock Springs.

Frigid temperatures occurred across the region. Three locations east of Rock Springs experienced low temperatures of minus 40 degrees or below, including minus 45 degrees at a site 8 miles East of Rock Springs.

Very heavy snow fell over a four day period across the Tetons. Many areas received over three feet of new snow with some areas exceeding four feet. Teton Pass was closed at times for avalanche control. Some of the snowfall totals included 58 inches at the Phillips Bench SNOTEL and 44 inches at the Jackson Hole Ski Resort.

Very heavy snow fell across portions of Yellowstone Park. The hardest hit areas where in the southwestern portions of the Park. Over 3 feet of snow fell in some locations, including 50 inches at the Lewis Lake Divide SNOTEL. Less snow fell in the north, where amounts generally ranged from 9 to 18 inches.
Heavy snow fell over most of the Absarokas. Some of the highest amounts included 32 inches and 30 inches at the Wolverine and Blackwater SNOTEL sites respectively.

Extremely heavy snow fell over the Salt and Wyoming Range. All SNOTEL locations reported at least three feet of snow with several topping four feet. Some of the highest totals included 56 inches at the Blind Bull Summit SNOTEL and 53 inches at the Spring Creek and Indian Creek SNOTELS.

Very heavy snow fell across the western slope of the Wind River Range. The highest total observed was 38 inches of the Kendall Ranger Station SNOTEL. The heavy snow combined with strong winds to close South Pass for several hours as well.

Very heavy snow fell across the eastern slopes of the Wind River Range. The highest snowfall totals recorded were 54 inches at the South Pass SNOTEL and 53 inches at the Deer Park SNOTEL. The snow combined with strong winds to bring significant blowing and drifting of the snow that made travel very difficult and resulted in the closure of South Pass at times during the event.

Very heavy snow fell over the Jackson Valley over four days. The highest amounts were 40 recorded, three miles SSW of Wilson and two miles west-southwest of Jackson. In the town of Jackson, the snow mixed or changed to rain at times and this held accumulations down to around 9 to 18 inches.
Very heavy snow fell across most of the region. The highest amounts were measured at Bondurant where 32.6 inches of new snow fell. Further south, around a foot fell near Pinedale.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Upper Green River Basin. At Big Piney, 10 inches of new snow was measured.
Heavy snow fell in southern Lincoln County. Some of the amounts included 9 inches at Kemmerer and 7 inches north of Cokeville.

Heavy snow fell throughout the Star Valley. The highest amounts were in the north and in the higher elevations where 29 inches fell at the Star Valley Ranch and 25 inches fell at Alpine. Further south, there was much less around Afton where the snow mixed and changed to rain for a time, limiting accumulation somewhat.

Heavy snow fell across northern Cody Foothills. The highest amount was at Pahaska where 22 inches fell. At Wapiti, 13 inches fell and 5 to 10 inches was measured through most of Cody. Very little snow fell further south around Meeteetse.

Heavy snow fell in a narrow band around the Lovell area. A foot of new snow was common with the highest amount of 19.1 inches. Amounts dropped off rapidly further south with less than three inches reported around Greybull.
The RAWS site at Fales Rock had many wind gusts past 58 mph; including a maximum of 78 mph. Other top winds gusts in the area included 76 mph at Camp Creek and 72 mph at Beaver Rim.
There were many wind gusts over 58 mph along Outer Drive south of Casper, including a maximum gust of 81 mph.
The ASOS at the Lander airport recorded a wind gust of 58 mph.
A 78 mph gust was measured at the weather sensor, five miles west-northwest of Clark.
The Teton County sheriff reported 6 to 8 inches of snow around the city of Jackson. In Moose, 9 inches of new snow fell.
Heavy snow fell throughout the Star Valley. Snowfall amounts ranged from 8.5 inches at Afton to 19.5 inches 5 miles north-northeast of Thayne.
Heavy snow fell through most of the Salt and Wyoming Range. Some of the highest amounts included 16 inches at the Willow Creek SNOTEL and 14 inches at the Kelly Ranger Station SNOTEL.
Heavy snow fell in the southern portion of Lincoln County. Some of the highest amounts included 12 inches at Cokeville and 11 inches at Diamondville.
The COOP observer in Riverton reported 10.3 inches of new snow. In Hudson, there was 11 inches of new snow.
The observer at the Lander airport measured 10.8 inches of new snow. Across Lander, new snow ranged from 9 to 11 inches.
New snow generally ranged from 8 to 10 inches. At Pinedale, 10.1 inches of new snow fell.
At the Jackson Hole Ski Resort, 19 inches of new snow was measured.
Snowfall amounts in the Upper Green River Basin ranged from 8 inches at Big Piney to 14 inches at Farson.
Snowfall amounts in the Green Mountains and Rattlesnake Range varied from 9 inches at Jeffrey City to 11.7 inches at Sweetwater Station.
The observer at the Casper airport measured 8.4 inches of new snow. Snowfall amounts around the city of Casper generally ranged from 6 to 9 inches.
Trained spotters measured 7 to 10 inches of new snow around the city of Thermopolis.
Trained spotters reported 12 to 15 inches around Green River. In Rock Springs, 6 to 9 inches of snow fell.
A 63 mph wind gust was recorded 8 miles south-southwest of Clark.
The RAWS at Camp Creek had several wind gusts past 58 mph; including a maximum gust of 65 mph.
An elderly man froze to death in his home, about 12 miles southwest of Cody, Wyoming. Temperatures outside were around -10 degrees on the morning of the 17th.
Rangers at Yellowstone National Park measured 18 inches of new snow at the east entrance to the Park and 13 inches at the Old Faithful Ranger Station.
Several locations of the Absaroka Mountains received over a foot of new snow. The highest amounts included 24 inches at Pahaska and 22 inches at the Beartooth Lake SNOTEL site.

Heavy snow fell in northern portions of the Cody Foothills. The highest amount was in Wapati where 13 inches of new snow fell. Around Cody, amounts generally ranged from 3 to 7 inches. Snowfall amounts dropped off rapidly further south.

Heavy snow fell in a narrow band across portions of Big Horn County. Almost 9 inches of snow was measured north of Shell with up to 6 inches around Greybull. North and south of this line snow fall amounts were much less.

A narrow band of heavy snow fell near Dubois. There were numerous reports of a foot of new snow with a maximum amount of 16 inches. Snowfall amounts fell rapidly further southeast with little snow reported at Crowheart.
Heavy snow fell in portions of Yellowstone Park. The highest amount recorded was 14 inches at the East Entrance to the park.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Absarokas. The highest amount recorded was 14 inches at the Beartooth Lake SNOTEL.
At the Jackson Hole Ski resort, 21 inches of new snow was measured.
Heavy snow fell in portions of Jackson Valley. Some of the highest amounts included 12 inches near Wilson and 10 inches near Teton Village.
A combination of snow, blowing snow and strong wind caused the closure of Wyoming Route 28 over South Pass for several hours.
A combination of snow, blowing snow and strong wind caused the closure of Wyoming Route 28 over South Pass for several hours.
The wind sensor west of Clark had several wind gusts past 58 mph, including a maximum of 76 mph.
Heavy snow fell through much of Yellowstone. The highest amount recorded was 18 inches at the Two Oceans Plateau SNOTEL site.

Very heavy snow fell in the Tetons. At the Jackson Hole Sky resort, 35 inches of new snow was measured. Other locations that received over 2 feet, included 27 inches at the Granite Creek SNOTEL and 26 inches at the Phillips Bench SNOTEL. In addition, snow, blowing snow and avalanches closed many major roads, including the roads at Hoback Junction and Highway 22 over Teton Pass.

Very heavy snow fell across the Salt and Wyoming range. The highest amount recorded was 32 inches at the Indian Creek SNOTEL. Other impressive amounts included 23 inches at the Willow Creek SNOTEL and 22 inches at Commissary Ridge.

Heavy snow occurred in much of the western slopes of the Tetons. The maximum snowfall amount was 20 inches at the Kendall Ranger Station. A combination of snow and strong wind closed South Pass for several hours as well.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Star Valley. Some of the heaviest amounts included 8 inches at Alpine and 6.5 inches at Afton.

Heavy snow fell throughout the Jackson Valley. The highest amounts were near Wilson, where 16 inches of new snow fell. Near the Jackson Dam, there was 9.5 inches of new snow. In Jackson, a very heavy snow load led to the collapse of the roof on the Sears Department Store. Near Teton Village, strong winds estimated over 70 mph, combined with heavy snow to down 17 power poles which led to a power outage lasting through the 11th. Jackson Hole Ski resort was closed through Monday the 13th.
Heavy snow occurred in portions of the Upper Green River Basin Foothills. The highest amount measured was 12.5 inches, 14 miles NW of Pinedale.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Cody Foothills. Around Wapati, Cody and Clark, 6 to 8 inches of new snow occurred. Snowfall amounts dropped rapidly further south.
High winds occurred in Sinks Canyon State Park near Lander. Several wind gusts past 58 mph occurred with a maximum gust of 72 mph.
The RAWS sites at Camp Creek and Fales Rock had several wind gusts past 58 mph, including a maximum gust of 75 mph at each site.
The wind sensor along Wyoming Boulevard south of Casper had several wind gusts past 58 mph, including a maximum of 65 mph.
High winds were recorded in many locations through the Green and Rattlesnake Range. The windiest spot was Camp Creek where a maximum wind gust of 94 mph was recorded.
The Kemmerer airport had a maximum wind gust of 59 mph.
High winds blew across portions of Eastern Sweetwater County. The maximum wind gust at the Rock Springs airport was 60 mph.
Heavy snow fell in portions of Yellowstone Park. The highest amount was at the Parker Peak SNOTEL where 20 inches of new snow fell.

Heavy snow fell in the higher elevations of the Tetons. Some of the highest amounts included 28 inches at the top of the Jackson Hole Ski resort, 18 inches at Grand Targhee and 16 inches at Togwotee Pass. This snow was heavy and moisture was dense. As a result, there were numerous avalanches throughout the Tetons. A series of avalanches closed Teton Pass and Hoback Junction several times between the 8th and 11th. An avalanche also closed Snow King ski resort on February 10th.

Up to two inches of rain fell onto deep snow pack in the Jackson Valley. The very heavy weight on roofs caused some minor damage to buildings, including to the police station. The rain also caused rapid snow melt that led to areas of minor flooding.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Absarokas. The SNOTEL site at Beartooth Lake had 17 inches of new snow.
Heavy snow fell in much of the western Big Horn Range. The highest amount of snow was 14 inches at the Big Sandy Opening SNOTEL site.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Salt and Wyoming range. The greatest amount of snow was 13 inches at the Spring Creek Divide SNOTEL.
Strong winds blew across much of the Green and Rattlesnake Range. At the RAWs at Camp Creek, there were many wind gusts past 60 mph, including a maximum of 82 mph.
There were numerous wind gusts past 58 mph along Outer Drive south of Casper, including a maximum gust of 69 mph.

Extreme winds occurred in the Cody Foothills around Clark. One wind sensor 5 miles WNW of Clark recorded many wind gusts of hurricane force including a maximum gust of 118 mph! A wind sensor to the south of Clark had a maximum gust of 87 mph.
High wind blew for several hours in Sinks Canyon State Park. The weather station had several gusts over 58 mph including a maximum of 69 mph.
The RAWS site at Sharpnose, 3 miles outside of Hudson, had several wind gusts past 58 mph, including a maximum gust of 73 mph.

Chinook winds warmed temperatures into the 50s early in the morning on the 10th and caused rapid snow melt that caused flooding in Lander. The flooding was concentrated around Baldwin Creek. Highway 287 between Lander and Fort Washakie was shut down for several hours. Water also flooded Smith Road, Main Street and Tweed Lane at times. Water surrounded some homes and forced a few evacuations. A few businesses as well as the Lander Museum experienced minor flooding during the event.

Chinook winds caused rapid snow melt in the Lander Foothills that brought rapid snow melt. The warm temperatures caused rapid snow melt that rapidly increased river levels. In addition, the frozen Little Popo Agie river broke up rapidly and ice jams caused flooding of the flood prone areas in Lyons Valley. Several homes and farms in the low lying areas experienced flooding and several side roads were flooded with a few washed out.

Chinook winds caused rapid snow melt in the Lander Foothills that brought rapid snow melt. The warm temperatures caused rapid snow melt that rapidly increased river levels. In addition, the frozen Little Popo Agie and Popo Agie rivers broke up rapidly and ice jams caused flooding of the flood prone areas in Lyons Valley. Many homes in the flood prone north and west sides of towns along with surrounding low lying areas were flooded. Many of the side roads in the aforementioned areas of Hudson also saw flooding and minor wash outs.

A combination of rapid snow melt from a chinook wind and ice jams caused the Little Wind River near Riverton to rise to 10.8 feet, 2.8 feet above flood stage. The water for the most part remained in low lying areas and caused little damage.

Rapidly warming temperatures after a prolonged cold spell, rapidly melted snow in the Big Horn Basin. This, combined with the frozen Big Horn River breaking up, produced flooding in Washakie County, especially in the vicinity of Worland. Over 100 homes were evacuated in the low lying residential areas along the river. Some residents were out of their homes for three days before finally being allowed back as the water receded on February 14th. The water receded after February 15th as the ice jam moved northward into Big Horn County.

Ice jams flowing northward out of Washakie County caused flooding in portions of Big Horn County along the Big Horn River from Manderson to Basin and north to Greybull. The flooding was mainly restricted to low lying areas along the river and caused little to no property damage.

Law enforcement reported flooding ditches and sheet flooding north of Riverton on the evening of February 21st. A 33-year old man fell into the flood waters and drowned. A Coroners report noted that the man was under the influence of alcohol, marijuana, amphetamines and anti-depressants.
A few wind gusts past 58 mph were recorded 5 miles west-northwest of Clark including a maximum gust of 71 mph.
Thr RAWS sites at Fales Rock and Camp Creek had several wind gusts above 58 mph including maximum gusts of 65 and 64 mph, respectively.
Several wind gusts past 58 mph were recorded along Outer Drive south of Casper including a maximum gust of 71 mph. The maximum gust at the Casper airport was 62 mph.
A 63 mph wind gust was measured at the Lander airport. A maximum wind gust of 65 mph was recorded at the weather station on the North Fork of the Popo Agie River.
An 80 mph gust was recorded 5 miles WNW of Clark.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Teton Mountains. The highest amount recorded was 13 inches at Granite Creek.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Salt and Wyoming Range. The highest amounts recorded was 15 inches at Blind Bull Summit.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Wind River Mountains. The highest amount recorded was 14 inches at the Little Warm River SNOTEL.
At the Lander airport, 16 inches of snow fell. Snowfall amounts around the Lander foothills generally ranged from 9 to 18 inches.

Heavy snow fell through portions of the Wind River Basin. At the Riverton airport, 13 inches of snow was measured with 9 to 12 inches through the city of Riverton. Further north, downsloping flow off of the Owl Creek Mountains kept accumulations lower. At Boyson Dam, there was 6 inches of snow.
A CocoRaHS observer measured 10 inches of snow at the Buckboard Marina.

Very heavy snow fell through Rock Springs and Green River. Amounts over a foot were common. The highest amount recorded was 23 inches in Rock Springs. Interstate 80 was shut down for a time due to the snow and drifting snow from gusty winds.

The Rock Springs airport had visibility drop to around a quarter of a mile and frequent wind gusts past 35 mph on February 23rd. These conditions led to nearly impossible travel conditions and closure of Interstate 80 for several hours.
A trained spotter measured 8 inches of snow in Wamsutter. Southeast of Rock Springs, 11 inches of snow was measured.
A CocoRaHS observer measured 7 inches of snow 4 miles southwest of Buffalo.

Heavy snow fell across portions of Natrona County. The heaviest snow fell in the western portions of Natrona County where Powder River picked up 13 inches of new snow. Amounts around the city of Casper generally ranged from 4 to 8 inches with 9.4 at the Natrona County airport. Much less snow fell in northern Natrona County where only 1 inch of snow fell at Midwest.
The SNOTEL on Casper Mountain reported 17 inches of new snow.
The weather sensor at Beaver Rim along Highway 28 reported visibility below a quarter of a mile and frequent wind gusts over 35 mph for several hours on the morning of February 23rd.

A long period of blizzard conditions occurred over South Pass with frequent wind gusts past 40 mph and heavy snow combined to bring white out conditions over Wyoming 28. The road was closed through this period.

A long period of blizzard conditions occurred over South Pass with frequent wind gusts past 40 mph and heavy snow combined to bring white out conditions over Wyoming 28. The road was closed through this period.
Heavy snow fell across the Green and Rattlesnake Range. The highest snow amount measured was 17 inches at Jeffrey City.

Very heavy snow fell across the East Slopes of the Wind River Range with amounts over two feet commonplace. Some of the highest amounts reported for SNOTELs included 34 inches at Townsend Creek and 28 inches at Deer Park. A COOP observer reported 26 inches of new snow at Atlantic City.
Trained spotters measured 6 to 9 inches around Farson. Snowfall amounts decreased further north in the zone.
A pair of 82 mph wind gusts occurred at the wind sensor along the Chief Joseph Highway.
Wind gusts to 67 mph occurred at the wind sensors 5 miles west-northwest and 8 miles south of Clark.
There were several wind gusts past 58 mph at Camp Creek; including a maximum wind gust of 77 mph.
The three wind sensors around Clark all recorded wind gusts past 58 mph. The strongest gust was 83 mph at the sensor 5 miles west-northwest of Clark.
A prolonged period of high wind occurred at the Camp Creek RAWS site. Wind gusts above 58 mph were recorded for over 24 hours straight including a maximum wind gust of 89 mph.
The ASOS at the Casper airport recorded a wind gust of 64 mph. Along Outer Drive south of Casper, there were several wind gusts between 55 and 60 mph.
The ASOS at the Lander airport reported a wind gust of 70 mph.
Trained spotters reported between 7 and 11 inches of snow through portions of the Star Valley. The highest amount reported was 11 inches at the Star Valley Ranch.
The ski patrol at Jackson Hole Ski Resort measured from 12 to 16 inches of new snow.
Several SNOTEL sites reported over a foot of new snow. The highest amount was 16 inches at the Blackwater SNOTEL.
The SNOTEL site at Parker Peak reported 12 inches of new snow.
The RAWS at Camp Creek had an extended period of high wind that continued for over 2 days. There were numerous wind gusts of hurricane force including a maximum gust of 87 mph.
The wind sensor along Outer Drive south of Casper recorded several wind gusts past 58 mph including a maximum gust of 68 mph.
The wind sensor along the Chief Joseph Highway reported several wind gusts past 74 mph including a maximum gust of 82 mph.
The emergency manager reported flooding along the Blacks Fork River near Granger and Little American. A mobile home park along the river was evacuated for 2 days but little or no damage was reported.
Sublette County Emergency Management reported flooding along portions of Highway 372 between Mile Markers 40 and 48. That portion of the road was closed for over 24 hours before the waters receded.
The Sublette County Emergency Manager reported a couple of houses had water in the basements along the Green River above the Fontenelle Reservoir.

Rain and warm temperatures brought rapid snow melt that brought minor flooding to some homes around Crow Creek near Fairview. Sandbagging was effective in diverting water around homes and there was no damage.

A combination of rainfall and warm temperatures caused rapid snow melt that brought flooding to some areas around Cokeville. The flooding was restricted to low lying agricultural land and caused no damage.
A combination of heavy snow and winds gusting over 45 mph at times brought blizzard conditions over South Pass. Highway 28 over South Pass was closed for over a day as a result.

A combination of heavy snow and winds gusting over 45 mph at times brought blizzard conditions over South Pass. Highway 28 over South Pass was closed for over a day as a result. Very heavy snow fell as well, with totals over 2 feet common and the maximum amount of 35 inches in the mountains southwest of Lander.
A combination of strong winds and snowfall led to the closure of Highway 287 between Highway 28 and Muddy Gap for several hours.

Heavy snow fell in portions of the Lander Foothills. The highest amounts were reported closer to the Wind River Range where some areas had over 10 inches. In the lower elevations, the snow mixed with rain at times and amounts where generally in the 6 inch range.
A 59 mph wind gust was reported at the Rock Springs airport.
Heavy snow fell from Riverton and southward. There were several reports of 6 to 9 inches of new snow. Amounts dropped sharply further north and west with Shoshoni only having 2 inches of snow.
The observer at the Lander airport measured 10.7 inches of new snow. Measurements of 6 to 9 inches were common around the city of Lander.
Heavy snow fell through much of the Tetons. The highest amounts of snow included 22 inches at the Grand Targhee SNOTEL and 20 inches at the top of the Jackson Hole Ski Resort.
The SNOTEL site at Gunsight Pass recorded 15 inches of new snow.

Heavy snow fell in portions of the Salt and Wyoming Ranges. Some of the highest amounts were at the Willow Creek and Cottonwood Creek SNOTEL sites where 20 and 18 inches of new snow fell, respectively.
Heavy snow fell in many portions of the Star Valley. Amounts ranged from 6 inches at the Box Y Ranch to 15 inches 5 miles SSE of Smoot.
Heavy snow fell over the east slope of the Bighorn range. The highest amount recorded was 19 inches at the Cloud Peak SNOTEL.

A narrow but intensive convective snow band developed over central Fremont County. Snow fell at rates of 2 inches an hour at times with wind gusts close to 60 mph at times. A NWS Employee measured 8 inches of snow about 5 miles NW of the Riverton airport with 6.2 inches of new snow in the city of Riverton. Amounts decreased rapidly outside of the band with generally 2 inches or less elsewhere.
Heavy snow fell along the eastern slopes of the Bighorn range. Some of the highest snowfall totals included 16 inches at the Hansen Sawmill SNOTEL and 15 inches at the Soldier Park SNOTEL.

Rain changed to a heavy, wet snow across northern Johnson County around midnight and quickly accumulated from 5 to 11 inches. The heavy, wet snow combined with gusty winds that knocked out power to much of Buffalo for several hours. At the height of the storm, portions of Interstates 25 and 90 were closed due to winter conditions.

Heavy snow fell across portions of the east slopes of the Bighorns. Numerous locations picked up over a foot of new snow. Some of the highest amounts included 18 inches at the Hansen Sawmill SNOTEL site and 15 inches at the Bear trap Meadow SNOTEL site.
Heavy snow fell in some of the higher elevations of the Absaroka Mountains. Some of the higher amounts included 25 inches at the Marquette SNOTEL and 19 inches at the Kirwin SNOTEL.
Heavy snow fell throughout the eastern slopes of the Bighorn range. Some of the highest amounts included 20 inches at the Little Goose SNOTEL site and 19 inches at the Soldier Park SNOTEL.
Trained spotters measured anywhere from 3.5 to 13 inches across Northern Johnson County, with the highest amounts in the foothills of the Bighorn range.
Anywhere from 6 to 12 inches of snow was measured across southern Johnson county.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Tetons. Some the highest amounts included 23 inches at the Jackson Hole Ski Resort and 29 inches at the Grand Targhee SNOTEL.

A CocoRAHS spotter reported 11 inches of snow at Moose. Snowfall amounts across the Jackson Valley were very elevation dependent with the city of Jackson only receiving 1.4 inches of snow since the snow mixed with rain at times.

A favorable moist upslope flow and chilly temperatures brought very heavy snow to the eastern slopes of the Wind River Range. There were several locations with over 2 feet of new snow with Townsend Creek having the most with 33 inches of new snow. A spotter at Atlantic City measured 24.5 inches of new snow. Even a bit lower in elevation, there was 17 inches of snow in Sinks Canyon State Park.

Heavy snow fell in portions of the Wind River Basin. The highest amounts were above 5500 feet with 9.9 inches of snow measured at WFO Riverton. Across the city of Riverton, there was anywhere from 4 to 8 inches of snow. However, since much of the snow fell during the daytime, there was never the total amounts of snow on the ground. In addition, many of the roads remained mainly wet through much of the event.

The official spotter at the Lander airport measured 7.7 inches of new snow. Snowfall amounts around Lander generally ranged from 2 to 6 inches with higher amounts closer to Sinks Canyon State Park. However, most of the main roads were mainly wet with the high late April sun angle melting the snow on paved surfaces.
A NWS Employee measured 8 inches of snow at Beaver Rim. 8 inches of snow also fell in Jeffrey City. During the height of the storm, US 287 was closed between Lander and Muddy Gap.

A trained spotter measured 7 inches of snow 5 miles south-southwest of Casper, in the foothills of Casper Mountain. Amounts dropped quickly closer to downtown where amounts were generally less than 3 inches.
At the Blind Bull SNOTEL, 15 inches of new snow fell. At Commisary Ridge, 21 inches of snow were measured.
The Cloud Peak SNOTEL site measured 12 inches of new snow.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Absaroka mountains. The highest amount recorded was 16 inches at the Marquette SNOTEL.
At the Casper Mountain SNOTEL 14 inches of new snow fell.

The official spotter at the Lander airport measured 6.3 inches of snow. Amounts were higher closer to the Wind River Range where some areas received over a foot. However, with the high May sun angle, most roads were just mainly wet to slushy.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the Green and Rattlesnake Range. The highest amount measured was 11 inches at Jeffrey City.
Heavy snow fell along the eastern slopes of the Wind River Range. Most areas received over a foot of new snow. The highest amount recorded was 20 inches at the Hobbs Park SNOTEL site.

There were numerous reports of a tornado just north of Interstate 80. The tornado lifted and touched down numerous times as it moved eastward. A motor home had it's windshield blown out by strong winds, and an 84 mph wind gust was reported at the weather sensor near Tipton.
A wind gust of 74 mph was measured at the Buffalo airport.
A 59 mph wind gust occurred at the ASOS at the Riverton airport.
A trained spotter reported nickel to quarter size hail, two miles east-southeast of Evansville.
The Natrona County emergency manager reported heavy thunderstorm rain, causing Webb Creek to overflow on Webb Creek Road on the evening of June 5th.
Multiple trained spotters reported hail up to the size of quarters in Evansville.
A motorist driving along Highway 789 south of Riverton reported hail up to the size of quarters.

High winds occurred across much of the Green and Rattlesnake Ranges. The highest winds occurred at Camp Creek where several gusts of hurricane force occurred with a maximum gusts of 86 mph. Some other notable gusts included 82 mph at Fales Rock and 66 mph at Beaver Rim.
Strong winds occurred in portions of Eastern Sweetwater County. The strongest gust was 63 mph at Bitter Creek.
High winds occurred in portions of the Rock Springs and Green River areas. The highest gust reported was 62 mph at the site on the west side of Rock Springs.
High winds occurred in portions of the Upper Green River Basin. The highest wind gust recorded was 67 mph at Farson. A 58 mph gust was recorded at the Big Piney airport.

Very strong winds occurred across the Lander Foothills. Some of the strongest winds included 76 mph at the Lander Airport and 75 mph at the North Fork of the Popo Agie River. The wind downed many trees in and around Lander and ripped the roof off of a garage.

A thunderstorm developed along the east side of the Bighorn Range and slowly strengthened. The storm became a supercell and dropped very large hail from Barnum to Kaycee. There were widespread reports of quarter size or bigger hail along the path. The largest report of hail was tennis ball size 5 miles southwest of Kaycee, not far from where a tornado developed. Hail up to the size of ping pong balls was reported in Barnum.

A storm survey was conducted near Kaycee and confirmed a tornado. The tornado touched down on a hill just west of Interstate 25 and just north of the Middle Fork of the Powder River. The tornado downed many trees moving down the hill. The tornado then strengthened as it crossed a field. An abandoned trailer was destroyed with the base thrown over 200 yards. Trees in the field were snapped off above the bases with some ground scouring noted. The tornado then crossed Barnum Road and moved northward toward Pine Ridge. The tornado narrowly missed a house and a barn as it moved up the ridge. Numerous trees were downed along both sides of the ridgeline before the funnel lifted. Winds were estimated at 110 to 120 mph, a minimal EF2 tornado.

A supercell thunderstorm dropped a weak rope tornado that moved slowly northward in southern Big Horn County and skipped along around a 3 mile path. The tornado remained over open country and caused no damage.
The public reported a tornado that briefly touched down several times in the Oregon Basin southeast of Cody. The tornado remained over open country and caused no damage.
The Natrona County emergency manager reported a brief tornado touchdown to the west of Bar Nunn. The tornado remained over open country and did little damage.
The public reported hail up to the size of half dollars around Evansville.
An off-duty NWS meteorologist reported a funnel cloud near the Trabing Road interchange of Interstate 25.
The public reported quarter size hail to the east of Ten Sleep.
The public reported hail up to the size of nickels in Midwest and Edgerton.
A CocoRaHS reporter reported flash flooding along Crazy Woman Creek near the south end of Espinoza Road south of Interstate 90.
The Sharpnose RAWS site recorded a thunderstorm wind gust to 61 mph.
A wind gust of 64 mph was reported at the DuBois airport.

The hardest hit areas were between South 10th and South 15th street as well as between Culbertson and Washakie Streets. A gust of 65 mph was measured at the Leigh Creek RAWS site.
A 59 mph wind gust was recorded at the Greybull airport.

There were numerous reports of hail across the Wind River Reservation from Ethete to near around Fort Washakie. The largest report was southeast of Arapahoe where hail of quarter size was reported.

Snow melt flowing downstream from the Absarokas brought flooding and high water along the South Fork of the Shoshone River. At the Ishawooa Bridge, downstream from Valley and near Aldrich Creek, the high water severely damaged the bridge. The bridge remained open, but was reduced to one lane while repairs were made. Waters receded on the 11th as cooler mountain temperatures slowed snow melt.
The South Fork of the Shoshone River crested at around 9.4 feet on June 18th and June 21st. The flooding remained in the low lands around the river and caused little to no damage.

Warm temperatures melted a well above normal snow pack in the mountains to the west of Dubois and led to flooding of the Wind River for a few weeks. There were two periods of flooding, the first from June 3rd through the 13th, and again from June 17th through the 24th. The River peaked at 5.7 feet, about 0.7 feet above flood stage. The flooding was largely across the low lying areas near the River and caused little or no damage.

Flood water from the Wind River and flowed across US 26 just to the west of Morton. The water covered the road to a depth of over a foot at times. This resulted in two different closures of the road, the longest of which lasted almost four days, stretching from afternoon of June 7th until around noon on June 11th.

Deep snow pack melted in the mountains and brought flooding along the Wind River near Crowheart, cresting at around 10 feet. The flooding occurred mainly in low lying areas near the river over rural areas and caused little damage.

Snow melt from the mountains produced flooding in the low lying areas near Kinnear. The flooding remained over low lying areas and agricultural land along the Wind River and produced little or no damage.

Abnormally large snowpack melted across the mountains of western and central Wyoming and caused the Wind River to Flood. At the Gauge at Riverton, the river crested above 12 feet, a new record. Along the Riverton Irrigation Canal, the water got high enough to flow directly into the canal, threatening the city of Riverton with flooding. The canal had to be breached to prevent the flooding. As a result, many farmers along the canal were left without irrigation water into July. The repairs to the canal cost around an estimated $2 million dollars. In addition, there was extensive flooding of agricultural land along the Wind River to it's confluence with the Little Wind River.
A trained spotter reported nickel size hail north of Teton Village.

Rain and rapid snow melt brought flooding along the Little Wind River. The most notable flooding was on the Wind River Reservation near Arapahoe. The water surrounded several homes along the River Bank, however, sandbagging efforts were successful and little property damage was noted.
Flooding was observed south of Riverton along the Little Wind River. Most of the flooding remained over the low lying areas near the river and no property damage was noted.
The Little Popo Agie River rose above flood stage for a few weeks. For safety reasons, the Lander Brewfest was moved from City Park. However, flooding caused little or no property damage.

Near Hudson, the Little Pop Agie River rose above flood stage for a few weeks. However, a flood wall that had been constructed in the previous weeks held and only some low lying areas flooded. As a result, there was little or no property damage.
The Middle Fork of the Popo Agie River went above flood stage for several days in June. Flooding remained in low lying areas and caused little to no property damage.
Emergency management reported flooding along the Greybull River. The flooding remained over low lying areas and caused little or no damage.
Emergency Managers reported flooding along the Big Horn River near Manderson. The flooding remained over low lying areas and caused no damage.

A severe thunderstorm crossed the border from Montana and brought up to golf ball size hail across much of northern Big Horn County. Lovell was the hardest hit community where there was widespread damage. One official estimated that over 60 percent of the homes had damage, mainly from damaged siding and broken windows from the hail bring driven by winds over 70 mph. Large hail was also occurred in Frannie and Cowley.

A severe thunderstorm brought high winds through much of northern Big Horn County. The strongest wind gust recorded was 79 mph at the Greybull Airport. Other notable gusts included 62 mph at Cowley and 59 mph at Frannie and Lovell. The strong wind combined with golf ball size hail to produce widespread damage across the city of Lovell.

A farm along Trabing Road reported broken windows, truck mirrors and damaged siding on a house and barn.

Snowfall amounts around Casper ranged anywhere from 2 to 8 inches, with the highest amounts closer to Casper Mountain. Heavy snow fell in the Tetons. The highest amount was 44 inches at the Jackson Hole Ski Resort. New snow amounts over two feet were common. The heavy snow caused numerous avalanches that shut down many roads for a time.
Heavy snow fell through much of the Jackson Valley. Amounts ranged from 6 to 12 inches around Jackson to around two feet in northern portions of the valley and near Teton Village.
Heavy snow fell in much of the Star Valley. Amounts ranged from around six inches in Afton to over a foot in the Foothills and closer to Alpine.

Strong winds occurred in portions of the Green Mountains. The strongest winds were at the highest elevations where wind gusts of 89 and 74 mph were recorded at the Fales Rock and Camp Creek RAWS sites, respectively. At Beaver Rim along Highway 28, a maximum wind gust of 76 mph was recorded.
High winds occurred along the south of side of Casper. Along Wyoming Boulevard, there were many wind gusts past 58 mph including a maximum gust of 67 mph.
Heavy snow fell throughout much of Yellowstone Park. Some of the highest amounts included 39 inches at the Two Oceans Plateau SNOTEL and 36 inches at the Lewis Lake SNOTEL.
Heavy snow fell through much of the Absarokas. Some of the highest amounts included 31 inches at Beartooth Lake at 29 inches at Pahaska.

Heavy snow fell through much of the Jackson Valley. Amounts of 10 to 20 inches were common with 30 inches reported near Wilson and 41 inches northwest of Moose.

Heavy snow fell in portions of the Green River Foothills. Areas around Bondurant had anywhere from 18 to 22 inches of new snow. Amounts dropped sharply further south with Pinedale only having one to two inches.

Trained spotters reported anywhere from 5 to 8 inches across Rock Springs, amounts generally diminished further to the west. The snow combined with winds gusting over 40 mph to cause the closure of Interstate 80 for several hours.
A trained spotter reported 10 inches of snow in Wamsutter. The snow combined with winds gusting past 40 mph to cause the closure of Interstate 80 for several hours.

Heavy snow fell through much of Natrona County. The highest snowfall amounts were closer to Casper Mountain where 12 to 18 inches of snow fell. The snow combined with winds gusting over 40 mph and brought the closure of some roads.

A combination of periods of snow and winds gusting past 50 mph at times brought the closure of roads, including Interstates 25 and 90.

Heavy snow fell in portions of southeastern Johnson County. The highest amount measured was 6 inches near Linch. The snow combined with winds gusting past 50 mph at times to bring near whiteout conditions and cause the closure of Interstate 25.

Heavy snow fell in portions of the Wind River Range. The highest amount was 19 inches at the Townsend Creek SNOTEL site.
An off duty NWS meteorologist reported anywhere from 6 to 9 inches of snow to the west of Beaver Rim.
Heavy snow fell throughout the Lander Foothills, with 10 to 20 inches of new snow commonplace. At the Lander Airport, 14,3 inches of new snow was measured.
Heavy snow fell along the eastern slopes of the Wind River Range. Some of the more notable amounts included 27 inches at the Townsend Creek SNOTEL site and 20 inches at the South Pass SNOTEL site.
Heavy snow fell in portions of the eastern Bighorn Mountains. At the Cloud Peak SNOTEL site 15 inches of new snow fell.
A trained spotter reported seven inches of snow about 13 miles south-southeast of Buffalo.
At the Lander Aiport, 7.7 inches of snow was measured. Around the region, amounts ranged from seven inches in Lander to 18 inches in Sinks Canyon State Park.

The Cloud Peak SNOTEL site received 16 inches of new snow.

NCRS reported the Middle Fork of the Powder River out of its banks in a few locations around Kaycee. The flooding was minor and no damage was reported.
NCRS employees reported minor to moderate flooding along the Middle Fork of the Powder River downstream from Barnum. The flooding remained over rural areas and caused no damage.
Heavy rain caused flooding in portions of Medicine Lodge state park.

The Riverton airport reached a record high temperature of 96 degrees. This was the all time record high temperature for September.

The Rock Springs airport reached a record high temperature of 90 degrees. This was the all time record high temperature for September and the first 90 degree high temperature ever recorded at the site in the month of September.
A 62 mph wind gust was reported at the Big Piney airport.
A 59 mph wind gust was reported at the Kemmerer airport.

Record cold temperatures occurred at the Greybull airport three nights in a row. The coldest temperature occurred on October 30th with a temperature of three degrees occurring. This record low temperature broke set an all time low for the month, which was nine degrees set in 2006.
Bitterly cold temperatures occurred in the Green Mountains. The coldest temperature recorded was 27 below zero at Jeffrey City, Wyoming.
Temperatures were very cold around the Upper Wind River Basin. Some of the notable temperatures on October 30th included minus 11 at Crowheart and minus 8 at the Dubois, Wyoming airport.

Record low temperatures occurred in the Wind River Basin. Temperatures around Riverton, Wyoming ranged from minus 5 to a low of minus 16 near Hudson, Wyoming. At the Riverton, Wyoming airport, the temperatures dropped to minus 9, setting an all time record low for the month of October. The old October record was 0 set in 2009.

Extremely cold temperatures occurred around the Lander, Wyoming Foothills. At the Lander, Wyoming airport on October 30th, the temperature dropped to minus 10, which broke the all time record low of minus 3 that occurred back in 1971.
Temperatures around Hot Springs county, Wyoming dropped as low as 10 below zero.

Many locations in northeastern Johnson County fell below zero, including minus 15 to the southeast of Story, Wyoming. At the Buffalo, Wyoming airport, a low of three degrees below zero was recorded, setting a new all time record low for the month of October.
Temperatures below zero were common across southern Johnson County. The lowest temperatures recorded was minus 9 at Linch, Wyoming on the morning of October 30th.

Extremely cold temperatures occurred in southern Lincoln County. Some of the coldest temperatures on the morning of the 30th included minus 26 at Fossil Butte National Monument and minus 20 just to the west of Kemmerer, Wyoming.
Very cold temperatures occurred in the Star Valley. Some of the coldest temperatures included minus 11 at the Afton, Wyoming airport and minus 9 at Thayne, Wyoming.

Very cold temperatures occurred through much of Natrona County. Some of the coldest temperatures included minus 20 west of Alcova, Wyoming and minus 15 at Evansville, Wyoming. At the Casper, Wyoming airport, the low of minus 9 on the morning of October 30th was the coldest temperatures ever recorded at the Casper, Wyoming airport, breaking the old record of minus 3 set in 1971.

Early morning, high based showers developed over the Tetons and moved into the Jackson Valley. A downdraft off of one of the shower caused 3 balloons to crash to the ground south of Teton Village. People were thrown from the baskets with the hard landings. In total 11 people went to the hospital, with 4 who were admitted and 1 that had to be evacuated by helicopter to a hospital in Idaho Falls.

Heavy snow fell throughout Natrona County, including 7.5 inches at the Casper Airport. The highest amount occurred on the south side of Casper near Casper Mountain, where over a foot of snow fell. The snow fell on trees with full foliage and combined with gusty north winds brought down numerous limbs that led to almost 3000 customers to lose power.

At the Lander, Wyoming Airport, 4.7 inches of snow fell. The snow fell on trees with full foliage and the result were downed limbs and in some cases entire trees. Over 600 customers were without power for a time.

A combination of snow and winds gusting to hurricane force brought nearly impossible travel conditions to eastern Sweetwater County. Winds gusted as high as 86 mph at the Sweetwater County airport. Interstate 80 was closed for a time during the height of the storm.

A tight pressure gradient and strong mid level winds mixed to the surface around Rock Springs and Green River, Wyoming. In addition, up to 7 inches of snow fell on trees that had full foliage. The result was widespread tree damage with large limbs and entire trees downed. At one point, almost the entire city of Green River along with much of Rock Springs, Wyoming was without power. Winds gusted as high as 67 mph in Green River at the height of the storm.
Wind gusts as high as 68 mph were reported in Farson, Wyoming. Some power lines were downed, leading to localized power outages.
The Sublette County emergency manager reported thousands of trees down throughout the western slopes of the Wind River Range.

The Sublette County Emergency Manager reported dozens of trees downed throughout the area. A messaging sign was blown down east of Pinedale, Wyoming. The sign was rated to withstand 82 mph wind gusts.

High winds downed many trees in Grand Teton National Park. Power was lost to many portions of the park with trails closed and some campers stranded in camp sites as roads were closed due to downed trees.

A strong cold front dropped through the Jackson Valley and mixed very strong mid level winds to the surface. The result was hundreds of trees downed through the area. Many subdivisions lost power for several hours in the surrounding areas. Trees were also downed in the city of Jackson, Wyoming, with the worst hit area near Albertson's where over a dozen trees were downed.

High wind occurred around the Cody Foothills. The strongest gusts were in the vicinity of Clark where a maximum wind gust of 79 mph was reported.
Nickel sized hail was recorded by a cooperative observer near Alta.
The ASOS at Riverton Regional Airport recorded a wind gust to 65 mph.  The damaging wind downed one large tree on the Central Wyoming College campus.
Hail of 1.25 inches in diameter was reported near Linch.
A thunderstorm that strengthened rapidly over downtown Riverton produced 0.75 to 0.88 inch diameter hail and a quick half-inch of rain.

Very strong wind downed a power line into a tree igniting a wildfire around 2215MST Monday, November 15, in the Line Creek area north of Clark. The starting point appeared to be in the 800 block of County Road 1AB. The wildfire rapidly spread through the Line Creek drainage, mainly the north side of the creek, as well as the area around Gunpowder Road as westerly wind gusting between 60 and 80 mph drove the flames eastward. The blaze, which eventually burned at least 300 acres, destroyed three homes, seven outbuildings, and a bridge. The fire was also responsible for the death of a 61-year-old woman who succumbed to smoke inhalation on Tuesday, November 16. Firefighters responded from across northern Park County and southern Montana to get the fire under control. Evacuations occurred for Louis L'Amour Lane and Crossfire Trail.

Very high winds occurred in the vicinity of Clark. A maximum wind gust of 95 mph was recorded. The highest wind gust in Cody was 64 mph.

A maximum wind gust of 62 mph was reported at Hunt Field in Lander.
High winds occurred around Casper. The maximum wind gust reported was 63 mph along Wyoming Boulevard along the south side of Casper.
High winds occurred in Johnson County after the passage of a cold front. The highest wind gust reported was 63 mph at the Johnson County Airport near Buffalo.
High wind occurred behind a cold frontal passage. Some maximum wind gusts included 62 mph at the Willow Creek RAWS and 58 mph at the South Big Horn County airport in Greybull.

High wind occurred across Natrona County. The maximum wind gust reported was 88 mph along Wyoming Boulevard on the south side of Casper. Other notable wind gusts included 77 mph at I-25 and Hat Six Road and 63 mph at the Casper-Natrona County International Airport. The high wind caused the collapse of a barn at the Central Wyoming Fairgrounds with 21 horses inside of it. Only 2 horses suffered scratches from the collapse.

A maximum wind gust of 68 mph was reported along Wyoming Highway 220 near Pathfinder Reservoir.

The ASOS at Southwest Wyoming Regional Airport east of Rock Springs recorded a peak wind gust of 62 mph.

A trained spotter reported 11 inches of snow to the southwest of Wilson.
